Quality Assessment

Two reviewers conducted an assessment of study quality using the criteria outlined, and any discrepancies were addressed through discussion. To ensure a robust quality assessment, we utilized specific criteria, including study design, sample size, assessment tools, and the clarity of reported results. Each study was scored based on these criteria to evaluate its methodological rigor and relevance to our review. Each study was individually assessed across four categories: sampling technique, predictive factors, and analysis. Studies that did not meet the preset criteria in these categories were omitted when drawing conclusions.

Data Extraction

Two reviewers independently extracted data from the studies using a standard template, including sample size, study design, participant characteristics, assessment scale, and predictor variables related to body satisfaction and acceptance.

Factors Associated with Likeliness to Pursue Cosmetic Surgical Procedure

Social media influence:The pervasive nature of social media platforms such as Instagram and Snapchat plays a crucial role in shaping individuals' decisions to undergo cosmetic procedures. These platforms are highly visual, emphasizing appearance through images and videos. Users are constantly exposed to idealized and often digitally enhanced images, setting high and sometimes unrealistic beauty standards. The constant comparison with these images can lead to dissatisfaction with one's appearance. The engaging and interactive features of social media, including likes, comments, and shares, further reinforce the desire to conform to these standards, driving individuals to consider cosmetic enhancements to align with the prevalent aesthetic ideals [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF5),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF14),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF17),[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF18),[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF19)].

Selfie behavior:The behavior of frequently taking and editing selfies has become a common trend, particularly among younger demographics. This practice is linked to higher considerations for cosmetic surgery. The process of taking selfies often involves scrutinizing one’s appearance closely, identifying perceived flaws, and using filters or editing tools to "improve" these features. Over time, this can lead to increased body dissatisfaction as individuals become more aware and critical of their imperfections. The desire to look better in selfies can translate into a willingness to undergo cosmetic procedures to achieve a more polished and attractive appearance that can be effortlessly captured on camera [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF4),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF15),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF20)].

Body dissatisfaction and anxiety:Anxiety over social appearance and body dissatisfaction are significant predictors of the desire to undergo cosmetic surgery. Individuals who are unhappy with their bodies are more likely to seek surgical solutions to improve their self-image. Social appearance anxiety, which involves the fear of negative evaluation of one’s appearance by others, exacerbates this desire. The pressure to meet societal beauty standards can lead to chronic anxiety and dissatisfaction, prompting individuals to consider cosmetic surgery as a way to alleviate these feelings and improve their confidence and social acceptance [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF2),[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF7),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF15)].

Cultural and societal norms: These factors heavily influence the perception of beauty and the acceptance of cosmetic procedures. In regions with high exposure to Western beauty standards, there is often a greater emphasis on certain aesthetic ideals, such as slim bodies, symmetrical facial features, and youthful appearances. These norms are propagated through various media, including movies, advertisements, and social media, creating a widespread belief in the desirability of these features. The pressure to conform to these standards can be immense, leading individuals to seek cosmetic surgery to fit the cultural and societal mold of beauty [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF21),[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF23)].

Celebrity influence:Celebrities play a significant role in shaping public perceptions of beauty and cosmetic surgery. Their endorsements and visible transformations are highly influential, particularly on social media. When celebrities undergo cosmetic procedures and publicly share their experiences and results, they normalize these practices and make them more desirable to the public. Followers who admire these celebrities may be motivated to undergo similar procedures to emulate their idols. The portrayal of flawless celebrity appearances as achievable goals can significantly sway individuals' decisions to pursue cosmetic surgery, viewing it as a legitimate and accessible means to enhance their own looks [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF5),[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF22),[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF25)].

Positive Attitudes Toward Cosmetic Surgical Procedure

Enhanced appearance: Many individuals view cosmetic procedures to improve their physical appearance. This perspective is rooted in the desire to address specific aesthetic concerns that may not be achievable through natural means. Whether it’s correcting perceived imperfections, reversing signs of aging, or enhancing certain features, cosmetic surgery provides a solution to attain desired looks. This enhancement can lead to increased self-esteem and confidence, as individuals feel more satisfied with their appearance. The notion that looking better can lead to feeling better is a significant driver behind the positive attitudes towards cosmetic procedures [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF1),[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF2),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF20)].

Social media validation: In the age of social media, achieving a certain look for online approval is seen as a benefit of cosmetic surgery. Platforms like Instagram and Snapchat place a high value on visual aesthetics, and users often seek validation through likes, comments, and shares. Cosmetic procedures can help individuals conform to the beauty standards prevalent on these platforms, thus enhancing their social media presence. The positive feedback received from followers can further boost self-esteem and provide a sense of social acceptance. For many, the ability to present an idealized version of themselves online is a compelling reason to undergo cosmetic enhancements [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF5),[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF14),[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF17)-[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF19)].

Emotional well-being: There is a belief that cosmetic surgery can lead to better emotional well-being despite the potential risks involved. For individuals who struggle with body image issues or have long-standing insecurities about their appearance, cosmetic procedures offer a way to alleviate these concerns. The satisfaction derived from seeing a more desirable reflection in the mirror can translate to improved mental health, reducing feelings of depression and anxiety related to body dissatisfaction. This improvement in emotional well-being is often cited by proponents as a significant benefit of cosmetic surgery [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF10),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF15)].

Negative Attitudes Toward Cosmetic Surgical Procedure

Risk awareness: Awareness of the potential physical and emotional risks associated with cosmetic surgery is a major factor contributing to negative attitudes. Complications from surgery, such as infections, scarring, and adverse reactions to anesthesia can deter individuals from pursuing these procedures. Moreover, the results of cosmetic surgery may not always meet expectations, leading to dissatisfaction and regret. The possibility of facing unmet expectations and the associated disappointment is a significant concern that fosters skepticism towards cosmetic procedures [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF6),[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF28)].

Body image issues: Concerns about fostering negative body image and unrealistic beauty standards are prevalent among critics of cosmetic surgery. The pursuit of an idealized appearance can perpetuate a cycle of dissatisfaction, where individuals continually find new flaws to fix. This focus on physical perfection can detract from the appreciation of natural beauty and individuality. Additionally, the promotion of certain beauty standards through cosmetic surgery can lead to societal pressures, making others feel inadequate if they do not conform. These issues highlight the potential negative impact of cosmetic procedures on overall body image [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF6),[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF15),[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11350482#REF20)].

Psychological impact: Elevated rates of depression, anxiety, and personality disorders are observed among those considering cosmetic surgery. The desire to undergo these procedures often stems from deeper psychological issues related to self-worth and identity. For some, the temporary boost in self-esteem provided by cosmetic enhancements may not address the underlying causes of their dissatisfaction. Instead, it can lead to a dependence on surgical solutions to manage emotional distress. args.summary: This is a systematic review published in Cureus (July 29, 2024) examining the relationship between social media use, body image dissatisfaction, and considerations for cosmetic surgery. The review, following PRISMA guidelines, included 25 studies with 13,731 participants. Key findings include: 70% of young adult women and 60% of young adult men report body dissatisfaction, leading to increased surgical considerations. Social media platforms like Instagram and Snapchat promote idealized and digitally enhanced images, fostering body dissatisfaction and social appearance anxiety—particularly through selfie culture. The review identifies several factors associated with interest in cosmetic surgery: social media influence, selfie behavior, body dissatisfaction and anxiety, cultural/societal norms, and celebrity influence. Positive attitudes toward cosmetic surgery are driven by enhanced appearance, social media validation, and emotional well-being. Negative attitudes stem from risk awareness, body image concerns, and psychological impact (depression, anxiety, personality disorders). The review notes that both men and women are affected, with cultural norms and celebrity influence shaping beauty perceptions. Ethical concerns about misleading advertisements, unrealistic beauty standards, and patient privacy are highlighted. The review underscores the need for strategies to promote healthy body image and informed decision-making in the digital age.

# The Rise of Cosmetic Surgery in the Social Media Era

## Unpack the troubling link between cosmetic surgery and the use of social media.

Posted February 11, 2025  |  [Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.](/us/docs/editorial-process)

* [![Share on Facebook](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/theme-assets/icons/icon-share-round-facebook-md.svg)Share](https://facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=220580041311284&display=page&href=https%3A//www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/no-more-fomo/202502/the-rise-of-cosmetic-surgery-in-the-social-media-era&redirect_uri=https%3A//www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/no-more-fomo/202502/the-rise-of-cosmetic-surgery-in-the-social-media-era "Share on Facebook")

### Key points

* Idealized images and celebrity endorsements on social media drive the desire for aesthetic procedures.
* Social appearance anxiety and body dissatisfaction lead many to seek cosmetic solutions.
* Clinicians, policymakers, and social media platforms must work together to promote body positivity.

![](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/article_inline_half_caption/public/field_blog_entry_images/2025-02/rise%20of%20cosmetic%20surgery.jpg?itok=z4p58yYC "Istock")

Source: Andrey Popov / Istock

Recent studies reveal that 70% of young adult women and 60% of young adult men are unhappy with their bodies. This troubling statistic coincides with the increasing normalization and availability of cosmetic surgery. In 2023 alone, Canadians underwent 35 million aesthetic procedures—a staggering 40% increase from four years prior. But what’s fueling this sharp rise? [Social media](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/social-media "Psychology Today looks at Social media") may be playing a pivotal role.

Researchers have uncovered a strong link between social media and the rise in cosmetic procedures. Apps like Instagram, Facebook, and Snapchat set unrealistic beauty standards through filters, influencer images, and celebrity transformations. Studies confirm that exposure to idealized bodies and edited photos, and the inevitable unfavorable social comparisons that result, drives individuals to pursue cosmetic surgery. A systematic review by Mironica et al. (2024) analyzed 25 studies involving nearly 14,000 participants and found that social media significantly influences decisions to undergo procedures. Similarly, Thawanyarat et al. (2023) noted a spike in cosmetic surgery searches after 2012, coinciding with Instagram’s rise.

## Celebrity Influence and Advertising

Social media has amplified the influence of celebrities in shaping beauty trends. When Kylie Jenner revealed her Juvederm lip injections, Google searches for dermal fillers skyrocketed. It’s not just celebrities—cosmetic surgery advertisements on social media play a crucial role. Thawanyarat et al. (2023) found that targeted ads significantly impact individuals’ decisions. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have become marketing goldmines for plastic surgeons, using hashtags like #plasticsurgery or #rhinoplasty to attract potential clients. These digital portfolios showcase cosmetic surgeons’ expertise while downplaying potential complications, capitalizing on users’ insecurities for monetary gain.

## Social Appearance Anxiety and the Pandemic Effect

Beyond advertisements and celebrity influence, social appearance [anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at anxiety")—the [fear](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/fear "Psychology Today looks at fear") of being judged on one’s looks—has fueled the demand for cosmetic procedures. Social media fosters constant comparison, leading many to feel inadequate. The [COVID-19](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/coronavirus-disease-2019 "Psychology Today looks at COVID-19") pandemic intensified these pressures, with video calls increasing self-scrutiny. A study by Padley (2022) found a surge in interest in cosmetic procedures, particularly for the face, as individuals became more aware of their appearance on screens. Many sought surgery as a way to regain [confidence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/confidence "Psychology Today looks at confidence") during this turbulent time. This is troubling given video conferences have become the norm in the post-pandemic era.

## Risks and Ethical Concerns

While cosmetic surgery can enhance appearance, it comes with significant risks. Social media promotes unrealistic beauty standards, with surgeons showcasing flawless results while never displaying botched outcomes, thus reflecting an unrealistic online reality. Physical risks include infection, scarring, and anesthesia complications, while emotional risks involve long-term dissatisfaction and regret. Critics worry about younger demographics seeking procedures prematurely, feeding into a cycle of [body image](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/body-image "Psychology Today looks at body image") issues and relentless self-modification that will only heighten with age. In fact, research shows that cosmetic surgery is a slippery slope, as undergoing one cosmetic surgery often leads to others in an attempt to “fix” other dissatisfied aspects of appearance.

## Moving Forward: Solutions and Awareness

To counteract these trends, clinicians should implement [body positivity](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/body-positivity "Psychology Today looks at body positivity") programs and screen patients for underlying psychological conditions like body dysmorphic disorder before procedures. Policymakers should regulate cosmetic surgery advertisements to prevent the promotion of unattainable beauty ideals and invest in mental health programs addressing [self-esteem](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/self-esteem "Psychology Today looks at self-esteem") and body image issues. Social media platforms have control over [advertising](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/consumer-behavior "Psychology Today looks at advertising") and should collaborate with mental health experts to promote more diverse, body-positive content and establish guidelines to reduce harmful beauty messaging.

Ultimately, users hold the power to shape their online experience. Curating a feed that celebrates [authenticity](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/authenticity "Psychology Today looks at authenticity") and self-acceptance can counteract social media’s pressures. However, algorithms can reinforce harmful beauty standards—engaging with cosmetic surgery content can lead to a constant stream of similar posts. The key question remains: do we truly need cosmetic enhancements, or are we being conditioned to believe we do? True self-worth comes from within, and fostering self-compassion is far more fulfilling than chasing an unattainable standard of perfection. This journey of self-acceptance takes time and effort but the benefits to emotional well-being will be much deeper than any scalpel can provide.

This Psychology Today article by Gary Goldfield, Ph.D., published February 11, 2025, examines the link between social media use and the rising demand for cosmetic surgery. Key points include:

- **Statistics:** 70% of young adult women and 60% of young adult men are unhappy with their bodies. In 2023, Canadians underwent 35 million aesthetic procedures, a 40% increase from four years prior.

- **Social Media Influence:** Apps like Instagram, Facebook, and Snapchat set unrealistic beauty standards through filters, influencer images, and celebrity transformations. A systematic review by Mironica et al. (2024) analyzed 25 studies with nearly 14,000 participants, confirming social media significantly influences decisions to undergo cosmetic procedures. Thawanyarat et al. (2023) found a spike in cosmetic surgery searches after 2012, coinciding with Instagram's rise.

- **Celebrity & Advertising Effects:** When Kylie Jenner revealed her Juvederm lip injections, Google searches for dermal fillers skyrocketed. Targeted ads on Instagram and TikTok use hashtags like #plasticsurgery to attract clients, while downplaying potential complications.

- **Social Appearance Anxiety & Pandemic:** The COVID-19 pandemic intensified self-scrutiny via video calls. A study by Padley (2022) found a surge in interest in cosmetic procedures, particularly for the face.

- **Risks:** Physical risks include infection, scarring, and anesthesia complications. Emotional risks involve long-term dissatisfaction and regret. Research shows cosmetic surgery can be a "slippery slope," with one procedure often leading to others.

- **Proposed Solutions:** Clinicians should screen for body dysmorphic disorder and implement body positivity programs. Policymakers should regulate cosmetic surgery ads. Social media platforms should promote diverse, body-positive content. Users are encouraged to curate feeds that celebrate authenticity and self-acceptance.

# Understanding the Influence of Social Media on Beauty Standards

Beauty standards have existed for centuries, evolving across cultures and historical periods. From the Renaissance ideal of curvaceous figures to the waif-like models of the 1990s, each era has shaped its own version of physical attractiveness. However, the rise of social media has drastically transformed how beauty is perceived, promoted, and pursued.

In this article we’ll talk about the role of social media in shaping beauty standards, analyzing its impact on self-perception, the beauty industry, and cultural ideals.

***Related:*** [***The Importance of Physiology in the Beauty Industry***](https://www.elitelearning.com/cosmetology/courses/the-importance-of-physiology-in-the-beauty-industry/)

![](https://www.elitelearning.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Cosmetology-Blog-Banner-1024x102.jpg)

## **The evolution of beauty standards**

Before the internet, beauty standards were shaped by magazines, television, and Hollywood celebrities. Fashion icons like Audrey Hepburn and Marilyn Monroe set the tone for beauty expectations, while later figures such as Kate Moss and Naomi Campbell influenced trends in the 1990s.

With the advent of social media, beauty standards have become more fluid yet more pervasive. Instead of a few dominant beauty ideals, there is now a globalized, algorithm-driven standard that rewards specific facial features and body types. The rise of high-resolution selfies, beauty filters, and plastic surgery trends has made social media an engine for both aspirational and artificial beauty.

A major shift has been the emergence of the **“**[**Instagram Face**](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/decade-in-review/the-age-of-instagram-face)**“**— a homogenous look characterized by plump lips, high cheekbones, flawless skin, and contoured features. This aesthetic, popularized by celebrities and influencers, is now seen across cultures, thanks to the viral nature of social media.

## **Influencers and brand strategies**

Many influencers promote specific beauty ideals, skincare routines, makeup techniques, and cosmetic procedures, often portraying a flawless image that can be difficult to achieve naturally. Beauty brands collaborate with these influencers to market their products, sometimes [reinforcing unrealistic expectations.](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/368017176_Impact_of_Instagram_Usage_on_Young_Women's_Body_Esteem_Mediating_Role_of_Beauty_Perception)

However, in response to criticism, there has been a shift toward authenticity. Some influencers and brands advocate for body positivity, self-acceptance, and unfiltered content. Campaigns like #NoFilter and #BodyPositivity aim to challenge traditional beauty norms and celebrate diverse representations of beauty.

## **The psychological impact of social media beauty standards**

The constant exposure to highly curated beauty content can lead to negative psychological effects, particularly among young users. [Studies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10471190/) have shown links between social media use and:

## **Cultural and societal perspectives on beauty**

Beauty standards vary widely across cultures, but social media has contributed to the globalization of certain aesthetic ideals. Western beauty standards, often characterized by slim bodies, clear skin, and symmetrical features, have been amplified worldwide.

However, many cultures are pushing back by promoting their own traditional beauty ideals and encouraging appreciation for [diverse beauty representations.](https://www.elitelearning.com/resource-center/cosmetology/gen-z-and-the-beauty-industry/)

Movements such as the natural hair movement in the Black community, the rise of K-beauty in Korea, and the celebration of different body types in Latin America highlight how different cultures navigate and redefine beauty standards in the digital age.

## **The role of technology in beauty enhancement**

Advancements in technology have further complicated the perception of beauty. AI-driven filters, deepfake beauty apps, and augmented reality (AR) tools allow users to drastically alter their appearance with just a few clicks. While these tools offer creative expression, they also contribute to body image dissatisfaction and unrealistic expectations.

The rise of cosmetic procedures, fueled by social media exposure, has also increased. Treatments such as lip fillers, Botox, and body sculpting are more accessible and normalized than ever. Many young users feel pressured to undergo these procedures to align with the digital beauty ideals they see online.

## **Promoting a healthier digital experience**

To mitigate the negative effects of social media beauty standards, individuals and platforms can take several steps:

## **Social media as a platform for change and diversity**

Despite its role in reinforcing unattainable beauty ideals, social media has also been instrumental in promoting body positivity and challenging traditional norms. The rise of diverse beauty representation, from different body types to skin conditions, is largely due to activists and influencers advocating for inclusivity.

[Winnie Harlow,](https://www.instagram.com/winnieharlow/?hl=en) a model with vitiligo, gained fame through Instagram before appearing on America’s Next Top Model. Unlike traditional models who fit conventional beauty standards, Harlow embraced her unique appearance, using social media to redefine beauty. Her success led to greater representation of skin diversity in fashion and advertising, proving that beauty is not one-size-fits-all.

The body positivity movement has also gained momentum, with hashtags like #EffYourBeautyStandards and #BodyNeutrality encouraging users to embrace their natural selves.

## **The future of beauty standards**

Social media plays a paradoxical role in shaping beauty ideals. While it has made beauty standards more globalized and, in some ways, unattainable, it has also given a voice to those who challenge conventional norms.

Moving forward, the landscape of beauty standards may continue to evolve with the rise of AI-generated influencers, virtual beauty trends, and greater awareness of mental health impacts. As users become more critical of filtered perfection, there is potential for a shift toward authenticity in beauty representation.

The question remains: can social media become a force for genuine self-acceptance, or will it continue to drive unattainable aspirations? The answer may depend on how both users and influencers choose to engage with these platforms in the years to come.

**Middle East and Africa Medical Aesthetic Market** **Definition**

Medical aesthetics includes all medical treatments that are focused on improving the cosmetic appearance of patients. Medical aesthetics sits in a beautiful little niche in between the beauty industry and plastic surgery. Qualified doctors, nurses, or dentists can provide a multitude of stunning treatments to improve your appearance. These treatments require a high degree of skill, training, and knowledge of your anatomy and physiology. This is what separates medical aesthetic treatments from beauty treatments such as eyebrow threading, waxing, or eyelash extensions. On the other hand, medical aesthetic treatments are not as aggressive as surgical interventions (aesthetic medical treatments are sometimes referred to as non-surgical cosmetic treatments), which includes procedures like facelifts, breast augmentations, or liposuction.

## **Middle East and Africa Medical Aesthetic Devices Market Size**

The medical aesthetic devices market size in the Middle East and Africa was worth USD 0.61 billion in 2024. The MEA market is estimated to be growing at a CAGR of 10.46% from 2025 to 2033 and be worth USD 1.49 billion by 2033 from USD 0.67 billion in 2025.

Medical Aesthetic Devices are used in minimally invasive or non-invasive cosmetic procedures, including laser and intense pulsed light (IPL) systems, radiofrequency devices, ultrasound-based skin tightening tools, injectable delivery systems, and energy-based fat reduction platforms. These devices are administered in clinical settings by licensed professionals to address skin rejuvenation, hair removal, body contouring, and facial aesthetics. According to research, a large number of minimally invasive procedures were performed in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, with botulinum toxin and laser treatments constituting the majority. Cultural emphasis on appearance, rising disposable incomes, and expanding dermatology infrastructure, particularly in urban centers like Dubai, Riyadh, and Johannesburg, have elevated the region’s significance in global aesthetic medicine.

## **MARKET DRIVERS**

### **Rising Influence of Social Media and Beauty Standards in Youth Demographics**

The pervasive influence of digital media and evolving beauty ideals among younger populations is contributing to the growth of the Middle East & Africa [medical aesthetic devices market](https://www.marketdataforecast.com/market-reports/medical-aesthetics-devices-market). According to a study, a portion of individuals in Saudi Arabia and the UAE actively use Instagram and TikTok, platforms where curated appearances and aesthetic procedures are widely promoted by influencers and dermatology clinics. This digital exposure has normalized non-invasive treatments, with a portion of women under 30 in the UAE having undergone at least one laser or skin rejuvenation procedure, according to research.

### **Expansion of Private Dermatology and Aesthetic Clinics in Urban Centers**

The proliferation of specialized aesthetic clinics across major metropolitan areas further drives the expansion of the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. As per the srudy, the number of licensed aesthetic and dermatology centers in the GCC increased, with Dubai and Riyadh serving as regional hubs. These clinics are equipped with state-of-the-art devices such as fractional CO2 lasers, cryolipolysis systems, and microneedling radiofrequency platforms. In Egypt, it reported a rise in private dermatology clinic registrations, driven by growing demand for hyperpigmentation and acne scar treatments.

## **MARKET RESTRAINTS**

### **Stringent Regulatory Gaps and Proliferation of Unlicensed Devices**

The inconsistent regulatory enforcement is a major factor holding back the growth of the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. This leads to widespread use of substandard or counterfeit aesthetic devices. According to research, a portion of medical devices in circulation in Nigeria and Pakistan are unapproved or falsified, with similar trends observed in non-regulated aesthetic clinics across West Africa. In Lebanon and parts of North Africa, the absence of centralized medical device registration allows uncertified lasers and RF machines to be imported and operated without clinical validation. The Saudi Food and Drug Authority seized a number of illegal aesthetic devices, including unbranded microneedling and cavitation units.

### **Cultural and Religious Sensitivities Influencing Procedure Acceptance**

Sociocultural norms in certain regions act as a barrier to the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. According to research, elective cosmetic procedures face resistance in conservative communities across Sudan, Yemen, and rural Pakistan due to religious interpretations that discourage bodily alteration. In some Gulf states, while facial and skin treatments are widely accepted, body contouring and injectables remain stigmatized among older demographics. Besides, gender-specific restrictions in some countries limit male access to dermatology services, despite rising demand for hair restoration. These sociocultural dynamics necessitate targeted education and culturally sensitive marketing, which slows the pace of market penetration in traditionally reserved populations.

## **MARKET OPPURTUNITIES**

### **Growing Medical Tourism in the GCC for Premium Aesthetic Treatments**

Rising medical tourism for premium aesthetic treatment in GCC, particularly in the UAE and Saudi Arabia, provides potential opportunities for the expansion of the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. According to a study, numerous international patients visited Dubai for cosmetic and wellness procedures, contributing notably to the healthcare economy. The Emirate has established dedicated medical free zones with streamlined licensing for international clinics, attracting global brands like Harley Street Aesthetics and Euromed. Saudi Arabia, under Vision 2030, is investing in luxury wellness resorts in NEOM that integrate advanced aesthetic technologies with holistic care. Medical tourism is projected to grow annually in the GCC in the coming years, as per the research, which creates demand for high-end laser, radiofrequency, and regenerative aesthetic devices.

### **Increasing Demand for Skin Hyperpigmentation and Scar Treatment Solutions**

The high prevalence of skin conditions such as melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and acne scarring, particularly among populations with darker skin tones, is giving new opportunities for the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. According to a study, pigmentary disorders affect a portion of individuals in Sub-Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, which creates a robust demand for safe, non-ablative laser and light-based therapies. Traditional high-energy lasers pose risks of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in Fitzpatrick skin types IV–VI, but newer devices with longer wavelengths and cooling mechanisms, such as picosecond lasers and fractional radiofrequency, are proving safer and more effective. This unmet dermatological need is driving investment in skin-type-specific device innovation and training for practitioners across the region.

## **MARKET CHALLENGES**

### **Shortage of Certified Aesthetic Practitioners and Standardized Training Programs**

The scarcity of formally trained professionals qualified to operate advanced aesthetic devices impedes the growth of the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. As per research, fewer practitioners performing laser and radiofrequency treatments hold certified credentials in aesthetic medicine. In Nigeria, a portion of aesthetic procedures are conducted by nurses or technicians without specialized dermatology training. This skills deficit increases the risk of adverse events, with a rise in laser burn cases. Thus, the credibility and scalability of the sector remain compromised due to the lack of standardized curricula and licensing.

### **High Import Tariffs and Supply Chain Fragmentation**

The fragmented and costly import infrastructure for medical aesthetic devices across the region continues to be a challenge for the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market. According to a study, import duties on medical devices in Lebanon, Egypt, and Algeria vary, which significantly inflates equipment costs. In Ethiopia and Tanzania, prolonged customs clearance processes delay device deliveries by weeks, as reported by the African Medical Device Trade Network. Furthermore, a lack of cold-chain logistics and voltage compatibility issues in rural clinics hinder deployment. These logistical and financial barriers deter global manufacturers from establishing direct distribution, which forces clinics to rely on third-party suppliers with limited after-sales support. This ultimately affects device maintenance, safety, and long-term adoption.

### **By Product Type Insights**

The energy-based devices segment led the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market and captured 54.1% share of the regional market in 2024. According to research, a portion of women in Cairo seek treatment for melasma or post-inflammatory pigmentation, driving athe doption of Q-switched and picosecond lasers. The proliferation of accredited dermatology clinics equipped with advanced energy systems strengthens their dominance across urban centers.

The anti-wrinkle products segment is likely to achieve the highest CAGR of 14.6% from 2025 to 2033. The increasing consumer focus on facial aesthetics, particularly among younger demographics seeking preventive treatments, is among the key factors accelerating the expansion of the anti-wrinkle products segment. Botulinum toxin injections, now commonly administered to individuals in their late 20s, are increasingly used to delay dynamic wrinkle formation. As per a study, a portion of women in Riyadh have undergone at least one neuromodulator treatment. Moreover, the introduction of longer-lasting formulations and combination therapies with dermal fillers has enhanced clinical outcomes.

### **By Procedures Insights**

The cosmetic procedures segment accounted for a significant share of the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market in 2024. The dominance of the cosmetic procedures segment in the regional market is fueled by strong cultural emphasis on appearance, rising disposable incomes, and the normalization of aesthetic enhancements through digital media. Non-surgical treatments such as laser skin resurfacing, chemical peels, and injectables constitute the majority, with a number of such procedures performed in the GCC. Besides, Dubai’s status as a regional aesthetic hub has led to the establishment of specialized clinics offering minimally invasive treatments. The reconstructive procedures segment is anticipated to witness the fastest CAGR of 11.8% between 2025 and 2035. Governments in Saudi Arabia and South Africa are integrating reconstructive care into public health programs, with Saudi Vision 2030 allocating funds for specialized centers, which signals institutional recognition and long-term growth potential.

The clinics segment dominated the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market and held a substantial share in 2024. The requirement for medical supervision in administering regulated aesthetic treatments such as laser therapy, injectables, and radiofrequency tightening is mainly propelling the growth of the clinics segment. Licensed dermatology and plastic surgery clinics in urban centers like Dubai, Riyadh, and Johannesburg are equipped with high-end devices and staffed by certified practitioners, ensuring compliance with safety standards. This regulatory framework ensures quality and builds consumer trust, which strengthens clinics as the primary delivery channel for advanced aesthetic care.

Also, the Kingdom is investing heavily in healthcare modernization, with the allocation of funds to develop specialized wellness and aesthetic centers in NEOM and Riyadh. According to research, many new aesthetic clinics received licensing, supported by relaxed regulations for foreign medical practitioners. The country’s youthful population is increasingly adopting preventive treatments, with botulinum toxin and laser hair removal being the most sought-after procedures.

The UAE occupies the second place in the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market and accounted for 24.4% of the regional market share in 2024. The Dubai Healthcare City Authority regulates many accredited aesthetic clinics, ensuring adherence to international safety standards. The presence of luxury wellness resorts,a high expatriate population, and aggressive marketing by global brands like Allergan and Lumenis further strengthen the UAE’s prominence. Regulatory clarity and digital health integration are accelerating the adoption of AI-assisted aesthetic platforms across private clinics.

South Africa experienced continuous growth in the Middle East & Africa medical aesthetic devices market because it is the most developed aesthetic healthcare ecosystem in sub-Saharan Africa. The country boasts a high concentration of board-certified dermatologists and plastic surgeons. According to a study, skin rejuvenation and pigmentation correction are the most common procedures, driven by the high prevalence of melasma among women of mixed ancestry. The private healthcare sector, which covers aa portion of the population, supports advanced device adoption, with Johannesburg and Cape Town clinics offering picosecond lasers and non-surgical body sculpting.

### **Egypt Medical Aesthetic Devices Market Insights**

# Middle East & Africa Medical Aesthetic Devices Market Report Summary

The Middle East and Africa (MEA) medical aesthetic devices market was valued at **USD 0.61 billion in 2024** and is projected to grow at a **CAGR of 10.46%** from 2025 to 2033, reaching **USD 1.49 billion by 2033** (from USD 0.67 billion in 2025).

## Key Market Drivers
- **Social media influence**: Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have normalized non-invasive treatments among younger demographics, particularly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
- **Expansion of private clinics**: Proliferation of licensed aesthetic centers in GCC cities like Dubai and Riyadh, equipped with advanced devices.

## Market Restraints
- **Regulatory gaps**: Unlicensed/counterfeit devices common in Nigeria, Pakistan, Lebanon, and North Africa; Saudi FDA seized illegal aesthetic devices.
- **Cultural/religious sensitivities**: Resistance to cosmetic procedures in conservative communities (Sudan, Yemen, rural Pakistan); gender-specific restrictions in some countries.

## Opportunities
- **Medical tourism in GCC**: UAE and Saudi Arabia attracting international patients; Saudi Vision 2030 investing in luxury wellness resorts.
- **Skin hyperpigmentation treatments**: High prevalence of melasma and acne scarring in darker skin types driving demand for safe, non-ablative laser and light-based therapies.

## Challenges
- **Shortage of certified practitioners**: Few trained professionals; many procedures performed by nurses/technicians without specialized training.
- **High import tariffs and supply chain fragmentation**: Import duties vary significantly across Lebanon, Egypt, Algeria; customs delays in Ethiopia and Tanzania.

## Segmental Analysis (2024)
- **By Product Type**: Energy-based devices led with 54.1% market share; anti-wrinkle products expected to grow at fastest CAGR of 14.6%.
- **By Procedures**: Cosmetic procedures dominated; reconstructive procedures expected to grow at fastest CAGR of 11.8%.
- **By End Users**: Clinics dominated; home-use segment expected to grow at fastest CAGR of 13.2%.

## Country-Level Insights
- **Saudi Arabia**: Top performer with 28.5% market share; driven by Vision 2030 healthcare modernization.
- **UAE**: Second with 24.4% share; Dubai as medical tourism hub.
- **South Africa**: Most developed aesthetic healthcare ecosystem in sub-Saharan Africa.
- **Egypt**: Rapid growth due to large population and evolving consumer behavior.
- **Israel**: Global leader in aesthetic device R&D (Pollogen, InMode).

## Key Market Players
Allergan, Cynosure, Johnson & Johnson, LCA Pharmaceutical, Galderma Pharma, Solta Medical, Cutera, Focus Medical, Human Med Ag, Genzyme Corporation, Alcon Inc., Alma Lasers, Lumenis, InMode.

## Medical Aesthetics Market Trends:

### ***Growing Demand for Non-Invasive Procedures***

The rising demand for non-invasive procedures is the primary driver of the market growth. In addition to this, the changing consumer preferences towards cosmetic enhancements are also driving the medical aesthetics market outlook. Furthermore, the increasing popularity of various beauty treatments, such as dermal fillers, Botox injections, and laser therapy is further boosting the market growth. For example, the Allergan 2022 report shows growing acceptance of non-invasive treatments, and the progress continues to emphasize delivering effective results with minimal downtime and less risk than traditional surgical procedures or even injectables. New muscles for treatment include the additional elbow and forearm muscles: brachialis, brachioradialis, pronator teres, and pronator quadratus. Nonetheless, technological advancements and the desire for minimal downtime have been major drivers for non-invasive procedures. The market grew by 6% for botulinum toxin procedures, whereas dermal fillers experienced growth of 4% in 2023. As a result, the usage of botulinum toxins in aesthetic medicine has remarkably surged. Botox injections are employed in the treatment of frown lines, crow's feet, and horizontal forehead lines. These are cosmetic indications which have been approved by the US FDA.

### ***Emerging Technology Trends***

Advancements in laser technology, injectables, and energy-based devices are major drivers in the development of the medical aesthetics market. This expansion is also due to their effectiveness and versatility in addressing increasingly sophisticated technologies for specific concerns related to the skin, like pigmentation, wrinkles, and tattoo removal. In addition, the popularity of longer-lasting and more natural-looking injectables has led to cosmetic enhancements becoming accessible and appealing to a wider range of people. For instance, GC Aesthetics is a well-established leader in breast aesthetics that collaborated with Bimini Health Tech, a pioneer in health care solutions, to revolutionize the world of breast reconstruction. There is immense growth in the medical aesthetics market. This is due to cultural changes that are more of self-confidence and seeking youthfulness. The regulatory authorities also approve various products, and this has enhanced the growth. For instance, Lumenis launched the Splendor X device in the United Kingdom in January 2022. It obtained CE clearance for hair removal, vascular issues, pigmented lesions, and wrinkles. The growing demand for botulinum toxin treatments, coupled with the growing number of aesthetically conscious individuals and an ongoing stream of new releases, is also fueling the growth of the market. Botulinum toxin is a neurotoxic protein found in Clostridium botulinum that acts by interrupting nerve impulses to the administered muscles upon injection. Apparently, the most common receivers of botulinum toxin type A cosmetic treatments are adults aged 31-45 years. # Medical Aesthetics Market Report Summary

## Market Overview
The global medical aesthetics market was valued at USD 6.46 billion in 2025, projected to reach USD 6.67 billion by 2026 and grow to USD 8.93 billion by 2035, at a CAGR of 3.29% (2026-2035). The report is authored by Payal Rabde, a healthcare market research analyst with 4+ years of experience, and was last updated on August 6, 2026.

## Key Market Segments
- **By Type**: Non-invasive procedures currently dominate the market; invasive segment is predicted to witness significant growth.
- **By Application**: Acne scar removal led the market in 2025; lip augmentation is expected to gain significant share.
- **By End-User**: Hospitals and clinics hold the largest market share, followed by beauty centers and spas.

## Regional Analysis
- **North America**: Largest regional market, driven by advanced infrastructure, high cosmetic procedure adoption, and skilled surgeons.
- **Asia-Pacific**: Fastest-growing region, fueled by rising surgeries, tech adoption, and medical tourism. Key countries: Japan, China, India, South Korea.
- **Europe**: Notable market driven by aging population and non-surgical procedure trends. Germany and UK are key markets.
- **Latin America**: Growing through medical tourism, especially Mexico (ranked 2nd globally for health tourism) and Brazil.
- **Middle East & Africa**: Growing region with UAE and Saudi Arabia showing rapid development.

## Growth Drivers
- Rising number of surgeries (approx. 35 million aesthetic procedures in 2023 per ISAPS)
- Technological advancements (lasers, AI, robotics)
- Growing demand for minimally/non-invasive procedures
- Increasing geriatric population
- Expanding medical tourism
- Rising beauty awareness and social media influence

## Key Market Players (Tier 1)
- **AbbVie (Allergan Aesthetics)** – Botox Cosmetic, Juvederm, CoolSculpting Elite
- **Galderma** – Restylane, Sculptra, Dysport
- **Merz Aesthetics** – Xeomin, Belotero, Radiesse, Ultherapy

## Recent Developments
- March 2026: Allergan Aesthetics announced "Undetectable Era" shift for hyaluronic acid injectables at AMWC Monaco.
- February 2026: Clear + Brilliant Touch laser launched in Canada by Bausch Health/Solta Medical.
- January 2025: Merz Aesthetics launched Ultherapy PRIME® in Europe.
- February 2025: Allergan Aesthetics opened three new U.S. training centers.

## Challenges
- High treatment costs and low reimbursements
- Stringent regulatory approvals (e.g., EU MDR 2017/745)
- Safety concerns regarding injectables
- Shortage of skilled practitioners
- Risk of implant malfunctions

## AI in Medical Aesthetics
AI is increasingly used for personalized treatment design, advanced diagnostics, realistic simulations, and predicting procedure outcomes, helping patients and physicians make informed decisions.

--- SOURCE 1: Self-Perceived Dental Esthetics and Orthodontic Treatment Need ---
URL: https://www.jrmds.in/articles/selfperceived-dental-esthetics-and-orthodontic-treatment-need-88601.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the Journal of Research in Medical and Dental Science (2021, Volume 9, Issue 12) titled "Self-Perceived Dental Esthetics and Orthodontic Treatment Need." The study was conducted by researchers from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Health and Umm Al-Qura University, led by Amjad Alotaibi.

**Objective:** To explore self-perceived dental esthetics of adults and evaluate their subjective orthodontic treatment needs on esthetic grounds.

**Methodology:** A descriptive, cross-sectional study using a self-administered questionnaire distributed randomly to the general population in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia. A total of 1,014 participants (737 female, 277 male, aged 18-60) completed the questionnaire, which included the Aesthetic Component of the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (AC-IOTN) and the Oral Aesthetics Subjective Impact Score (OASIS).

**Key Findings:**
- 66.5% of participants had positive self-perceived dental esthetics (mean OASIS score: 12.53 ± 7.34, range 5-35).
- According to AC-IOTN self-evaluation: 90.1% had "no need" for orthodontic treatment, 5.1% had "borderline need," and 4.7% had "definite need."
- A statistically significant positive correlation was found between OASIS and AC-IOTN scores (r=0.37, p=0.005), indicating that as concern about dental esthetics increased, perceived orthodontic treatment need also increased.
- Gender significantly influenced the demand for orthodontic treatment, with females more concerned about appearance.
- Prior studies cited in the article note that professional assessments identify much higher orthodontic treatment needs (71.6% severe need) compared to self-perceived needs.

**Conclusion:** The study found a weak association suggesting that when esthetic self-satisfaction decreases, the subjective need for orthodontic treatment increases. The authors recommend that patients' perceptions of their own dental esthetics and gender differences should be considered in orthodontic treatment planning.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The positive association indicated that as the individual's OASIS score increased, suggesting a greater concern about dental esthetics, his or her orthodontic treatment needs also increased on the AC-IOTN."; "The demand for orthodontic treatment was significantly influenced by gender."; "A comparison of these estimates to professional assessment indicates that only 15.2% have little or no need for treatment, 13.2% have a moderate/borderline need, and 71.6% have a definite need for treatment."; "The present study suggests that the majority of adult individuals have positive self-perceived dental esthetics, and that the demand for orthodontic treatment is significantly influenced by gender."; "It is important to consider the patient's perception of his or her own dental esthetics along with gender differences in orthodontic treatment planning."

--- SOURCE 3: Profiles of facial soft tissue changes during and after orthodontic treatment in female adults ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9233845

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in BMC Oral Health (2022), used 3dMD stereo photography technology to investigate facial soft tissue changes during and after orthodontic treatment in 52 adult Chinese females (24 extraction, 28 non-extraction cases). The research aimed to determine whether "braces face" (thinner faces, protruding cheekbones, sunken temples) is a real orthodontic effect or due to excessive patient attention, and to identify factors associated with these changes.

**Key Findings:**
- Overall facial soft tissue protrusions reduced by about 2 mm on average during orthodontic treatment, regardless of extraction status. Negative changes (~1 mm reduction) occurred in infraorbital, cheekbone, zygomatic, sub-zygomatic, lower cheilion, buccal, mandibular angle, and temporal regions.
- Extraction was **not** a major factor for facial soft tissue changes. Changes were consistent between extraction and non-extraction groups, with only the temporal region (R11) showing statistically significant differences between the two groups.
- Negative changes in the buccal region (R9) moderately correlated with shorter distances of nasion-menton and subnasale-menton, and larger ratios of face height to face width, indicating that adult females with **wide and short faces** may be more prone to negative soft tissue changes.
- An increase in posterior facial height (N-Go distance) was identified as a risk factor for negative changes in the zygomatic arch area (R3).
- A moderate positive correlation was found between maxillary first molar width changes and negative changes in the lower cheek region (R9) (rs = 0.41, P < 0.05), suggesting that narrower dental arch width correlates with more obvious lower cheek depression.
- Soft tissue changes were detectable as early as 3 months after treatment initiation but did not necessarily worsen thereafter.

**Conclusions:** Short face height, long mid/lower face width, and large face height-to-width ratios are major factors for aesthetic risks. Changes in posterior facial height and first molar arch width are also risk factors. Extraction is not a primary cause of facial soft tissue changes.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: The impact of orthodontic treatment on face and smile attractiveness: A cross-sectional study of longitudinal data ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0889540626001563

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article published in the American Journal of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopedics (Volume 170, Issue 2, August 2026, Pages 262-273) titled "The impact of orthodontic treatment on face and smile attractiveness: A cross-sectional study of longitudinal data."

**Objective:** To assess the effect of orthodontic treatment on facial and smile attractiveness as perceived by laypeople.

**Methods:** The study included 37 adults (aged 21-35 years): 29 treated patients and 8 untreated controls. A total of 132 photographs (full-face smiles and close-up smiles) were collected pre- and post-treatment for treated patients and once for controls. Laypeople (n=297) rated the images using a visual analog scale (VAS). Statistical analyses included univariate regression models, analysis of covariance, t-tests, and Spearman correlation.

**Key Results:**
- Orthodontic treatment significantly improved facial attractiveness by 15.6% (P<0.001) and smile attractiveness by 24.3% (P<0.001) on VAS scores.
- Post-treatment ratings were higher than untreated controls (P_face=0.029; P_smile=0.010), with no significant differences at baseline.
- Higher Aesthetic Component of the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN-AC) scores correlated with lower initial VAS ratings (r=0.67; P<0.001).
- Age and treatment duration had no significant effect on attractiveness ratings.
- Evaluator demographics (including history of orthodontic treatment) did not significantly influence ratings.

**Conclusions:** Orthodontic treatment improves facial and smile attractiveness as perceived by laypeople, supporting its esthetic benefits for patient communication and treatment planning.
</summary>

# Dental Aesthetic Integration: Enhancing Facial Harmony Through Smile Alignment

This article from drmmacdonald.com explores the integrated approach of dental aesthetics, emphasizing that a beautiful smile exists as part of a larger facial ecosystem. ## Key Scientific Foundations

- **Facial types**: Research using computer analysis of 91 facial images identified four main facial types—strong, dynamic, delicate, and calm—with a C5.1 classification tree algorithm achieving 84.3% accuracy in prediction. Notably, 61.5% of people have features of two facial types, and 38.5% have features of three, underscoring the need for highly customized treatment.

- **Digital technology**: Digital Smile Design (DSD) uses high-resolution photography and specialized software to simulate dental outcomes before clinical work begins. 3D modeling and facial mapping allow clinicians to analyze facial features, measure proportions, and assess how the smile line aligns with the lower lip curve.

## Treatment Options and Sequencing

The article details a comprehensive range of procedures with expected longevity:
- **Porcelain veneers** (10-20 years): Thin custom shells that correct chips, cracks, discoloration, and reshape the smile line
- **Teeth whitening** (6-12 months): Professional brightening that enhances overall complexion

--- SOURCE 12: Clear aligners’ effects on aesthetics: evaluation of facial wrinkles ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6057070

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This retrospective cohort study published in the Journal of Clinical and Experimental Dentistry (2018) by Romeo Patini et al. evaluated the effects of clear aligner orthodontic treatment on lower third facial ageing in adult patients. The study compared a treated group (TG) of 68 patients using Invisalign clear aligners to a control group (UG) of 33 untreated patients. Each group was divided into subgroups based on age: under 40 (subgroup 1) and over 40 (subgroup 2). Facial aesthetics were assessed using the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale (WSRS) at baseline (T0) and after an average of 12 months (T1) by a panel of five calibrated aesthetic experts.

Key results: In the younger subgroups, TG1 showed a statistically significant WSRS improvement of -0.21 (p<0.05) while UG1 worsened by 0.27 (p<0.05), with a between-group difference of -0.29 (p<0.05). In the older subgroups, TG2 improved by -0.28 (p<0.01) and UG2 worsened by 0.30 (p<0.05), yielding a highly significant between-group difference of -0.65 (p<0.001). The anti-aging effect was more pronounced in older patients.

The authors propose two mechanisms for this effect: (1) a "splint effect" from wearing two 0.75mm aligners for 22 hours/day, which slightly increases vertical intraoral dimension, reducing muscular activity and intra-articular compression; (2) cellular and molecular changes in bone and muscle structures from mechanical signals, potentially involving mechano-growth-factor (MGF) and insulin growth factor 1 (IGF-1) release.

Study limitations include a relatively small sample size, reliance on photograph-based evaluations, and lack of a traditional braces control group (excluded because brackets could create a confounding lifting effect on wrinkles). The authors conclude that clear aligner therapy provides a modest but beneficial anti-aging effect on the lower third of the face, particularly in older patients.
</summary>

This is a research article published in BMC Oral Health (July 2, 2025) titled "The impact self-esteem towards the orthodontic issues in the social media: a cross-sectional study." The study investigates how social media usage affects self-esteem, self-perceived aesthetics, and perceived need for orthodontic treatment across three generational groups: Generation Z (born 1997–2012), Generation Y/Millennials (born 1980–1996), and Generation X (born 1965–1979).

**Methods:** Cross-sectional observational study with 250 participants from Brazil. Data were collected via self-administered questionnaires distributed through social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, WhatsApp) during March-April 2024. The questionnaire covered background characteristics, social media usage patterns, self-perceived aesthetics (using a Visual Analog Scale), and self-esteem (using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, RSES).

**Key Results:**
- Generation Z reported the highest average daily social media use (4.42 hours), followed by Generation Y (3.28 hours) and Generation X (2.65 hours).
- Generation Z reported significantly greater negative impact of social media on work/studies, and significantly higher tendencies to compare body appearance and life experiences with others compared to Generations Y and X.
- No significant generational differences were found in self-perceived dental aesthetics, orthodontic treatment need, or self-esteem scores.
- Generation Z had the lowest mean self-esteem score (21.84), though not statistically significant.
- A moderate negative correlation (r = -0.489) was found between satisfaction with dental appearance and perceived need for orthodontic treatment.
- Female participants compared body appearance and life experiences significantly more than male participants.
- Self-esteem showed weak negative correlations with social comparison tendencies.

**Conclusion:** No significant generational differences in perceived orthodontic treatment needs were found. However, Generation Z exhibited higher social media usage and greater social comparison regarding body image and life experiences, indicating social media may contribute more significantly to social pressures among younger generations. Individuals with lower satisfaction in dental aesthetics perceived a higher need for orthodontic treatment.

This 2024 study published in *BMC Oral Health* (PMCID: PMC10908024) assessed orthodontic treatment demand, prior experience, and knowledge about fixed and aligner treatments among young adults (aged 18–30) in Poland and Chile.

### Methodology
- Cross-sectional questionnaire study (25 questions) delivered via social media over 3 months (July–September 2022)
- Target sample: >400 per country; 1,092 responses obtained (670 from Chile, 422 from Poland)
- Response rate: 1.99%
- The survey was exempted from bioethical committee approval (ref: RWP/6546/2022P)

### Key Findings on Treatment Demand
- **Prior orthodontic treatment**: 42.9% in Poland vs. 25.0% in Chile had been treated
- **Planning treatment within a year**: 11.8% in Poland vs. 5.3% in Chile
- **Overall**: 51.6% of all respondents did not want orthodontic treatment; 16.5% were unsure
- 20.6% of all respondents would rely on doctor's recommendation for appliance type; 14.7% were interested solely in aligners
- 58% of respondents had heard about aligners

### Patient Preferences
- **Direct-to-consumer services (without doctor)**: Not acceptable to 85.1% (Poland) and 64.8% (Chile)
- **Treatment without doctor supervision**: Unacceptable to 85% (Poland) and 65% (Chile)
- **Consultation by a general dentist vs. orthodontist**: Opinions were divided (about 38% said no in both countries)
- Most important treatment features: acceptable price (69.4%), expected excellent result (66.3%), treatment time (57.5%), aesthetics (45%)

### Knowledge Gaps
- Most young adults provided incorrect answers about various aspects of aligner treatment
- Only ~23% knew the correct daily wear time for aligners (22–24 hours)
- Only ~20% knew teenagers with mixed dentition could be treated with aligners
- 46.5% correctly believed aligners are indicated only for non-complex malocclusions
- In Chile, top recognized brands: Invisalign (43.9%); in Poland: Dr. Smile (52.8%)
- Main information sources: Chile relied on orthodontists/dentists/associates; Poland relied on social media

### Conclusions
- Patients in both countries demand treatment and monitoring by orthodontists
- A high percentage of patients want treatment exclusively with aligners
- Direct-to-consumer orthodontics is not attractive to patients
- Young adults lack adequate knowledge about aligner treatment
- Many people want treatment despite having undergone prior orthodontic treatment
- Poland and Chile show similar socioeconomic/developmental indices but cultural differences influence treatment demand and knowledge

- China's oral medical service market was ~270 billion RMB in 2023, with orthodontics (~540 billion) and dental implants (~610 billion) as the largest segments.
- Growth has slowed: 15% CAGR (2015-2019), under 10% (2019-2022), ~5% (2022-2024). Causes include penetration rate increases, competition, and specific events (collective procurement, consumption downgrade).

- **Orthodontics:** Growth stalled from 2022-2024. As a non-essential service, demand is highly sensitive to disposable income. Birth rate decline pressures the youth market.
- **Key divergent views:** Consumption downgrade impact is stronger than expected; non-essential services for men and young adults are hit hardest. Dental implants will still grow due to price-volume effects. The dental service industry is in a phase of overcapacity and price competition, with upstream players possessing mature overseas channels likely to succeed.
- **Upstream market:** ~25.2 billion RMB in 2023, growing at 13% CAGR. Growth varies by sub-segment: preventive/filling materials follow service volume; implants and orthodontics were high-growth leaders; older products (e.g., removable dentures) are declining.
- **Future outlook:** Implant fundamentals are stronger than orthodontics. Ideal industry growth rate is ~10%, but varies significantly by sub-sector.

**Part 2: Health Checkup Industry**
- Market size: 228 billion RMB (2019) → 272 billion (2022), CAGR 6.1%. Private sector grew faster at 15.5% CAGR (2019-2022).
- Post-COVID demand surge was temporary. Growth has slowed/stagnated since 2023 due to macroeconomic pressures.
- **Key divergent views:** The high-growth era is over. Profitability is challenged. Customer segmentation: state-owned/social insurance (40%), private enterprises (30%), individual (30%). Economic downturn is reducing enterprise spending on employee checkups. Price wars are intensifying.

- **Competition:** CR3 (top 3 private players) ~34.4% of 1.18 billion checkup visits in 2023. Price competition is severe. Net profit margins are low (most below 10%, some losses).
- **Financing:** Active investment in 2020-2021 (19-18 deals, 21.8 billion RMB peak) declined sharply in 2023-2024 (4-2 deals, 1.6 billion RMB).
- **Future outlook:** Favorable factors: aging population, e-commerce channel growth, integration with health management/insurance. Unfavorable factors: economic downturn, low entry barriers (capital/resources vs. technology), low net margins (~45% gross margin, <10% net margin).

**Conclusions:** Patient satisfaction is primarily driven by aesthetic improvements and effective communication. Financial concerns and social discomfort negatively affect the experience. The study highlights the importance of patient education, accessibility, and comprehensive support in optimizing orthodontic care outcomes.

This 2024 study published in *BMC Oral Health* (PMCID: PMC10908024) assessed orthodontic treatment demand, prior experience, and knowledge about fixed and aligner treatments among young adults (aged 18–30) in Poland and Chile.

### Methodology
- Cross-sectional questionnaire study (25 questions) delivered via social media over 3 months (July–September 2022)
- Target sample: >400 per country; 1,092 responses obtained (670 from Chile, 422 from Poland)
- Response rate: 1.99%
- The survey was exempted from bioethical committee approval (ref: RWP/6546/2022P)

### Key Findings on Treatment Demand
- **Prior orthodontic treatment**: 42.9% in Poland vs. 25.0% in Chile had been treated
- **Planning treatment within a year**: 11.8% in Poland vs. 5.3% in Chile
- **Overall**: 51.6% of all respondents did not want orthodontic treatment; 16.5% were unsure
- 20.6% of all respondents would rely on doctor's recommendation for appliance type; 14.7% were interested solely in aligners
- 58% of respondents had heard about aligners

### Patient Preferences
- **Direct-to-consumer services (without doctor)**: Not acceptable to 85.1% (Poland) and 64.8% (Chile)
- **Treatment without doctor supervision**: Unacceptable to 85% (Poland) and 65% (Chile)
- **Consultation by a general dentist vs. orthodontist**: Opinions were divided (about 38% said no in both countries)
- Most important treatment features: acceptable price (69.4%), expected excellent result (66.3%), treatment time (57.5%), aesthetics (45%)

### Knowledge Gaps
- Most young adults provided incorrect answers about various aspects of aligner treatment
- Only ~23% knew the correct daily wear time for aligners (22–24 hours)
- Only ~20% knew teenagers with mixed dentition could be treated with aligners
- 46.5% correctly believed aligners are indicated only for non-complex malocclusions
- In Chile, top recognized brands: Invisalign (43.9%); in Poland: Dr. Smile (52.8%)
- Main information sources: Chile relied on orthodontists/dentists/associates; Poland relied on social media

### Conclusions
- Patients in both countries demand treatment and monitoring by orthodontists
- A high percentage of patients want treatment exclusively with aligners
- Direct-to-consumer orthodontics is not attractive to patients
- Young adults lack adequate knowledge about aligner treatment
- Many people want treatment despite having undergone prior orthodontic treatment
- Poland and Chile show similar socioeconomic/developmental indices but cultural differences influence treatment demand and knowledge
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: The Impact of Orthodontic-Related Social Media Content on Patients’ Willingness to Initiate Treatment: A Systematic Review ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2304-6767/14/5/263

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This systematic review (published in Dentistry Journal, Volume 14, Issue 5, May 2026) evaluates the impact of orthodontic-related social media content on patients' willingness to initiate orthodontic treatment. The review was conducted by Lappas et al. from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, following PRISMA guidelines and Cochrane methodology.

**Methods:** An extensive literature search across five databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, Scopus, ProQuest) up to August 2025, plus manual reference screening. From 1,243 records identified, eight studies met inclusion criteria: six cross-sectional studies, one randomized controlled trial, and one qualitative study. Narrative synthesis was used due to heterogeneity.

**Key Findings:**

1. **Content Type:** Before–after photographs of completed orthodontic treatment were the most persuasive content type, consistently associated with increased willingness to seek treatment and higher perceived credibility. Technical content (e.g., screws, elastics) received the lowest ratings.

2. **Platform Effects:** Instagram was identified as the most influential platform across multiple studies.

3. **Gender Differences:** Female participants were more responsive to social media exposure than males across multiple studies.

4. **Treatment-Specific:** Clear aligner therapy content was particularly effective; 95% of participants in one study reported social media influenced their consideration of aligner therapy.

5. **Decision-Making:** 73.3% of participants considered searching social media important before seeking orthodontic treatment. Online reviews, follower counts, and third-party endorsements influenced treatment decisions.

6. **Credibility:** Before–after posts and teaching-related content received highest credibility ratings; 79.1% of participants would trust their clinician more if the clinician maintained an active social media profile.

**Conclusions:** Visually oriented social media content, particularly before–after imagery, shows consistent associations with willingness to seek orthodontic treatment. However, the evidence base is predominantly cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. The authors recommend further well-designed studies to better understand the mechanisms of social media influence on orthodontic treatment decisions.

**Study Details:** Authors include Konstantinos Lappas, Efthymia Tsialta, Nefeli Katanaki, Ioanna Pouliezou, and Iosif Sifakakis (corresponding author). The review was published open access under CC BY license (DOI: 10.3390/dj14050263).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Social media appears to influence patients' willingness to seek orthodontic treatment, although this effect is not consistent across individuals or content types. Visual content, particularly before–after images, was most strongly associated with increased willingness and perceived credibility. Female users demonstrated greater responsiveness to social media exposure. Instagram was identified as the platform exerting the strongest influence. The current evidence base is limited and consists predominantly of cross-sectional studies, which limits causal inference.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article titled "Evaluation of augmented reality and social media on patient motivation to undergo fixed orthodontic treatment" published in APOS Trends in Orthodontics (2024, Vol. 14, Issue 2, pp. 124-129). The study, conducted at Pravara Institute of Medical Sciences, Maharashtra, India, evaluated how augmented reality (AR) filters and social media influence patient motivation for orthodontic treatment.

**Methods:** 300 subjects (159 female, 141 male) visiting the orthodontic department completed questionnaires before and after viewing AR simulations. Patients were shown a Snapchat filter simulating a "braces look" and the SmileView filter (by Invisalign India) showing their probable post-treatment smile. Responses were rated on a 1-5 scale.

**Key Results:**
- 42% of patients were more enthusiastic about orthodontic treatment after seeing SmileView results
- Most respondents (38.3%) were moderately motivated to undergo treatment after seeing themselves with braces on filters (P < 0.0001)
- AR had a statistically significant positive effect on patient attitudes toward orthodontic treatment (P < 0.001)
- 42.7% were very satisfied with their simulated post-treatment smile
- Most respondents were not heavily influenced by social media comments/followers

**Conclusions:** AR can help patients overcome dental anxiety about fixed orthodontic treatment through exposure therapy and by providing a positive goal. Visual simulations positively influence patient interest, motivation, and satisfaction. The study suggests AR can improve patient communication, education, and engagement in orthodontic practice.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in the Medical Research Archives (European Society of Medicine) on 30 November 2024, investigates the motivations, expectations, and understanding of patients and their parents seeking orthodontic treatment in specialist practices in Beed, India. A total of 200 questionnaires (100 for patients, 100 for parents/guardians) were distributed, with closed-ended questions covering three domains: motivation, understanding, and expectation of orthodontic treatment.

Key findings include:
- Referral for orthodontic treatment was initiated by the patient's general dental practitioner in the majority of cases.
- The anticipation of improved dental appearance was the prime motivating factor.
- 92% of patients and parents showed a strong preference for metal braces; ceramic braces had only 2% acceptance, and aligners (e.g., Invisalign) had 6% acceptance.
- Only 12% of parents had initiated the consultation themselves, while 30% of patients stated their parents had initiated the referral, indicating a communication gap.
- Both patients and parents had realistic expectations overall, but were less well-informed about the nature and duration of orthodontic retention.
- Many parents believed orthodontic treatment would positively impact confidence and self-esteem.

The study concludes that orthodontic practitioners should improve communication and education regarding treatment options and long-term retention to better meet patient and family needs. The study's strength lies in its primary care specialist practice setting, which is more reflective of typical orthodontic patient experiences compared to hospital-based studies.
</summary>
