# Clear Aligners Market Summary

## Market Overview & Size
The global clear aligners market was valued at **USD 4.66 billion in 2025**, estimated at **USD 5.58 billion in 2026**, and projected to reach **USD 13.65 billion by 2031**, growing at a **CAGR of 19.59%** during the forecast period (2026-2031). The study period covers 2020-2031.

**Key Market Metrics:**
- **Fastest Growing Region:** Asia-Pacific (21.11% CAGR through 2031)
- **Largest Market:** North America (44.85% revenue share in 2025)
- **Market Concentration:** Medium
- **Major Drivers:** Rising adult malocclusion, chair-side 3D printing adoption, hybrid DTC-clinic models, AI-driven treatment planning, biocompatible smart polymers, and expanding regulatory reimbursement

## Segment Highlights

**By Age:** Adults held 74.58% of market share in 2025. Teens are the fastest-growing segment at 21.58% CAGR through 2031, driven by products like Invisalign First and Bluetooth wear-time sensors.

**By Manufacturing Workflow:** Centralized lab production accounted for 79.55% of 2025 market share. In-office chair-side 3D printing is growing at 22.05% CAGR, reducing turnaround times and material waste by up to 40%.

**By Material:** Multilayer polyurethane captured 67.62% of market in 2025. PET-G is forecast to grow at 21.92% CAGR, benefiting from superior thermoforming fidelity and easier recycling compliance with EU single-use plastic directives.

**By End User:** Stand-alone practices generated 61.40% of 2025 revenue. Hospitals are projected to grow at 21.35% CAGR through 2031.

**By Distribution Channel:** Offline channels accounted for 55.70% of 2025 revenue. Online platforms are poised to grow at 23.02% CAGR through 2031, driven by hybrid DTC-clinic models.

## Key Market Drivers
1. **Rising adult malocclusion** (4.2% CAGR impact) - Adults aged 18+ accounted for 37% of new orthodontic starts in 2025, up from 28% in 2019.
2. **Chair-side 3D printing** (3.8% CAGR impact) - Reduces treatment cycle times and material waste.
3. **Hybrid DTC-clinic models** (3.5% CAGR impact) - Acquisition costs dropping by up to 40% vs. brick-and-mortar-only.
4. **AI-driven treatment planning** (3.1% CAGR impact) - Align's ClinCheck reduced refinements from 32% to 19%.
5. **Biocompatible smart polymers** (2.9% CAGR impact)
6. **Regulatory reimbursement expansion** (2.4% CAGR impact)

## Key Restraints
- High capital cost of digital workflow software (up to USD 50,000/year, plus up to USD 100,000 for equipment)
- Limited evidence for complex Class III skeletal corrections
- IP litigation and patent expirations (-1.5% CAGR impact)
- Emerging plastic-waste regulations (-1.3% CAGR impact)

## Geographic Insights
- **North America (44.85% revenue):** Strong insurance schemes, dense orthodontist network, Align Technology's dominance
- **Asia-Pacific (21.11% CAGR):** Fastest-growing; Chinese adoption at only 11% vs. 33.1% in US; domestic challengers scaling automated lines
- **Europe:** Steady gains under EU MDR; sustainability directives driving material innovation
- **Middle East & Africa / South America:** Gradually opening through private insurance and government initiatives

## Competitive Landscape
**Major Players:** Align Technology, Angelalign Technology, SmileDirectClub, Straumann Group, Envista Holdings

Three strategic clusters emerging:
1. **Premium innovators** - AI-assisted planning, complex-case protocols, proprietary polymers
2. **Cost leaders** (China/India) - Fully automated production at less than half US price points
3. **Hybrid channel players** - Virtual onboarding, physical scan hubs, affiliated dentists

## Recent Developments (2026)
- **June 2026:** Straumann Group raised 2026 profitability guidance (140-170 bps core EBIT margin expansion)
- **May 2026:** Align Technology announced new manufacturing facility in Hyderabad, India (expected 2027)
- **April 2026:** Align Technology previewed Invisalign Palatal Expander system with integrated 3D-printed technology at AAO 2026
- **April 2026:** FDA 510(k) K260722 cleared on April 15, 2026
- **December 2025:** ITC Section 337 investigation instituted involving Align Technology and Angelalign Technology

## Regulatory Notes
Clear aligners are regulated as Class II medical devices under FDA 510(k) pathway in the US. EU MDR mandates post-market surveillance. UK's General Dental Council (2024) requires clinical exam before any aligner prescription.

## Future Outlook
Key opportunities include scaling provider-centric DSO workflows, faster international expansion by non-US incumbents, and bundling interoperable planning software with open-scanner compatibility. Angelalign reported 532,400 case shipments in 2025 (256,200 from global markets outside China, with 82.1% growth in those regions).

## Abstract

(1) Objective: This study aimed to investigate how patients’ perceptions of their dental aesthetics and their sense of self-esteem are related. (2) Methods: This cross-sectional survey recruited 141 new patients seeking orthodontic treatment. Patients completed a self-administered questionnaire consisting of three parts: the Malaysian Psychosocial Impact of Dental Aesthetics Questionnaire (PIDAQ), Rosenberg Self-esteem Scale (RSES-M), and Aesthetics Component of the Index of Orthodontics Treatment Need (IOTN-AC). Clinical assessment comprised the Dental Health Component of the Index of Orthodontics Treatment Need (IOTN-DHC). Multiple linear regression was performed, with self-esteem as the dependent variable, while the independent variables comprised the domains of PIDAQ; IOTN-AC; IOTN-DHC; and patients’ demographics, such as age, gender, and their level of education. (3) Results: The response rate was 96.5% (n = 136 respondents). The multiple linear regression found that, when the other predictors in the model are held constant, Social Impact, Aesthetic Concern, and Dental Self-Confidence are the factors that significantly contributed to explaining the variation in self-esteem, accounting for, 3.9%, 2.3%, and 2.0%, respectively. The entire model explained 23% of the variation in self-esteem. (4) Conclusions: Domains of the psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics act as predictors of self-esteem in orthodontic treatment-seeking patients.

## 1. Introduction

Malocclusion, or problems with dental arrangement, is a global issue. The worldwide prevalence of malocclusion is 56%, regardless of gender [[1](#B1-healthcare-12-01576)]. There is substantial evidence regarding the epidemiological significance of malocclusion. Therefore, malocclusion is a significant oral health issue and an economic burden for both the families of affected children and public dental health services.

Orthodontic treatment has anecdotally been perceived to service the demand for addressing problems relating to dental aesthetics. Generally, treatment need for orthodontics is often evaluated by clinicians using normative need indicators [[2](#B2-healthcare-12-01576)], which often provide insufficient patient input on the effects of the dental aesthetics on their oral health, emotional, and social factors. The need for orthodontic treatment to manage malocclusion is associated with the oral health-related quality of life in children and adolescents. A systematic review has suggested two potential factors, namely gender and self-esteem, that could modify this relationship [[3](#B3-healthcare-12-01576)].

Dental aesthetics, influenced by factors like tooth color, form, and alignment [[4](#B4-healthcare-12-01576)], significantly impact adolescents’ psychological well-being and self-confidence [[5](#B5-healthcare-12-01576),[6](#B6-healthcare-12-01576)]. Patients who sought orthodontic treatment have been recorded to have a higher psychosocial impact, particularly lower self-confidence [[7](#B7-healthcare-12-01576)] than the general population [[6](#B6-healthcare-12-01576)] and those who have had orthodontic treatment. Factors that motivate patients to seek orthodontic treatment include wanting to improve their self-image, concerns about aesthetics, and wanting to improve their confidence and to remove their negative thoughts about their teeth [[8](#B8-healthcare-12-01576)].

The Psychosocial Impact of Dental Aesthetics Questionnaire (PIDAQ) [[9](#B9-healthcare-12-01576)] is a useful tool to assess psychosocial impact related to malocclusion that could support clinical parameters in determining the priority of treatment for patients with malocclusions [[10](#B10-healthcare-12-01576)]. Such a validated and reliable instrument could be used as the yardstick to rank patients in terms of priority and expedite treatment to patients with higher psychosocial needs and has the propensity to maintain good oral health during treatment, when the clinical need is comparable [[11](#B11-healthcare-12-01576)].

Self-esteem is the belief in our own value and is crucial for mental well-being. Dental aesthetics are potential factors that can impact self-esteem [[12](#B12-healthcare-12-01576)]. Poorly aligned teeth or an aesthetically displeasing smile can lead to self-consciousness, reduced confidence, and social anxiety. Peers and social media influence self-esteem. Self-esteem is likely to be lower among those who are unable to adjust to external pressures for personal advancement [[13](#B13-healthcare-12-01576)]. For some patients with poor dental aesthetics, an improvement in self-esteem might be anticipated as one of the benefits of orthodontic therapy [[14](#B14-healthcare-12-01576)]. However, the evidence for improvement in self-esteem following orthodontic treatment is low [[15](#B15-healthcare-12-01576)]. This systematic review also reported that the influence of patients’ gender or age on self-esteem after orthodontic treatment is still not clear.

The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale is a recognized tool for self-esteem evaluation [[16](#B16-healthcare-12-01576)]. It has been widely used for measuring global self-esteem. The translated scale (RSES-M) has been shown to be a valid and reliable scale for measuring the level of self-esteem among Malaysians [[17](#B17-healthcare-12-01576)].

Self-perceptions of smiles and dental aesthetics have been shown to influence the self-esteem of adolescents [[18](#B18-healthcare-12-01576)]. However, a previous study found that social factors associated with dental aesthetics were found to be the only significant predictor of self-esteem [[19](#B19-healthcare-12-01576)]. The authors related this finding to their culture, wherein other people’s opinion is considered more important than their own. It is unclear whether this can be extended to other populations with varying cultures. Clinical indicators such as malocclusion have been related as causes for low esteem. Adolescents with Class II and III malocclusions reported lower levels of self-esteem scores compared to Class I malocclusion. Thus, there is a need to investigate how malocclusion and other factors, such as oral health-related quality of life, affect self-esteem. The null hypothesis is that there is no significant association between the domains of psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics and the level of self-esteem of patients seeking orthodontic treatment.

Therefore, the objectives of the study were (1) to assess the prevalence, extent, and severity of PIDAQ among patients seeking orthodontic treatment, as well as the level of their self-esteem; (2) to investigate the relationship between the psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics and the self-esteem of patients seeking orthodontic treatment; and (3) to assess the predictive value of the PIDAQ domains on the level of self-esteem. Presumably, the severity of their self-perceived malocclusion and their current self-esteem can be used to identify individuals who are strongly motivated to have orthodontic treatment.

## 2. Materials and Methods

This was a cross-sectional study conducted among patients who were seeking orthodontic treatment at the Faculty of Dentistry, Universiti Malaya. Inclusion criteria were patients who (1) seek orthodontic treatment aged from 12 to 50 years old, (2) have not undergone any orthodontic treatment before, (3) have no language barrier and are able to comprehend English and/or Malay, and (4) have an absence of any craniofacial anomalies. The study was conducted upon ethical approval from the Medical Ethics Committee of Faculty of Dentistry, Universiti Malaya (DF PD2212/0038; 2 April 2022). Respondents were recruited from March 2022 to August 2022.

According to an a priori sample size calculator for multiple regression, at least 118 respondents were needed for an anticipated medium effect size (f2 = 0.15), 10 predictors, a power level of 0.80, and a probability of 0.05 [[20](#B20-healthcare-12-01576)].

### 2.1. Study Instruments

Questionnaires comprising four sections were self-administered when the patients came for initial consultations at the orthodontic clinic with the postgraduates. The questionnaires were given after consent was given and before the respondents were seen for their orthodontic consultation session. The first section collected demographic information, such as name, age, gender, and education level.

The second section comprised the 22-item Malaysian version of the PIDAQ [[21](#B21-healthcare-12-01576),[22](#B22-healthcare-12-01576)] to determine the effects on oral health-related quality of life (OHRQoL) caused by dental arrangement. It assesses three negative domains—Social Impact (SI; 8 items), Psychological Impact (PI; 6 items), and Aesthetic Concern (AC; 2 items)—in addition to a positive domain—Dental Self-Confidence (DSC; 6 items). A 5-point Likert scale, with score 0 meaning “not at all” and score 4 meaning “very strongly”, was used to record the degree of agreement on each item.

The Malaysian version of the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES-M) [[23](#B23-healthcare-12-01576)] was used to determine the respondents’ self-esteem score in the third section. It comprises five positive and five negative items. Respondents self-rated the 10 items on a 5-point scale, with 0 signifying “strongly disagree” and 4 signifying “strongly agree”. Respondents with scores below 20 were considered to have low self-esteem [[24](#B24-healthcare-12-01576)].

The fourth section used the Aesthetic Component of the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN-AC) to evaluate the respondents’ personal impression of their malocclusion severity. On a scale of one to ten, where one represented the most appealing dental appearance and ten represented the least, respondents were asked to rank their perceptions of their dental aesthetics to determine their self-perceived malocclusion (SPM) [[25](#B25-healthcare-12-01576),[26](#B26-healthcare-12-01576)]. In addition, the orthodontic postgraduates, who had been trained on the use of the Dental Health Component of the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN-DHC), clinically assessed for the severity of their malocclusion and thus their need for orthodontic treatment [[25](#B25-healthcare-12-01576)]. The postgraduates undergo annual recalibration for the use of the IOTN as part of the curriculum at this institution for screening of all patients.

### 2.2. Data Analysis

[Table 1](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t001) shows the definitions and score range for the terms used in this study [[6](#B6-healthcare-12-01576),[16](#B16-healthcare-12-01576),[25](#B25-healthcare-12-01576),[26](#B26-healthcare-12-01576)]. Overall, only five respondents were removed from analysis due to incomplete demographic information.

**Table 1.**
Definitions and score range of the terms.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

For data analysis, the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (version 27.0; SPSS, Chicago, IL, USA, III) and Winsteps (version 3.80.1; Winsteps, Beaverton, OR, USA) were used; statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

The Shapiro–Wilk tests, Skewness, and Kurtosis distribution were used to determine whether the distribution of the data was normal. The Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests for multiple comparisons were conducted to compare variations in PIDAQ, self-esteem, SPM, and levels of malocclusion severity. For the IOTN-DHC, none of the respondents was rated as grade 1, while respondents with grades 4 and 5 were grouped together for analysis due to a low number of respondents with grade 5. Ordinal scales were converted to interval scales by Rasch analysis [[27](#B27-healthcare-12-01576)]. Self-esteem scores between genders were compared using an independent t-test, while one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare self-esteem scores between the age groups. The association between malocclusion severity, SPM, PIDAQ, and self-esteem were evaluated using Pearson correlation coefficient. The level of respondents’ self-esteem was tested using multiple linear regression analysis to see if the four PIDAQ domains, as well as age, gender, education level, and the IOTN-DHC and IOTN-AC, significantly predicted a certain level. The model’s multicollinearity was tested using the variance inflation and tolerance factors.

## 3. Results

[Table 2](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t002) shows the respondents’ profiles. Overall, 136 patients participated in the survey (response rate, 98.6%). There were 50 (36.8%) male and 86 (63.2%) female respondents, with a mean age of 22.4 years (SD: 6.8; range: 12 to 45 years). A majority of respondents (n = 71; 52.2%) were between 20 and 29 years old. About a third (n = 53; 39.0%) self-perceived themselves as having slight malocclusion, 41 (30.1%) as having moderate malocclusion, and 15 (11.1%) as having severe malocclusion, while 27 (19.9%) did not perceive themselves as having malocclusion. In contrast, when the malocclusion severity level was assessed using IOTN-DHC, as rated by clinicians, only seven (5.1%) respondents were in grade 5 (indicating very great need). Many of the respondents (n = 92; 67.6%) were in grade 4 (indicating great need), followed by grade 3 (indicating moderate need) with 24 (17.6%) respondents, and 13 (9.5%) respondents were in grade 2 (indicating little need). For the highest education level among the respondents, 9 (6.6%) have postgraduate qualifications, 60 (44.1%) were degree holders, 17 (12.5%) have a diploma, 47 (34.6%) have up to a secondary-school level of education, and only 3 (2.2%) respondents have a primary level of education.

The psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics of patients seeking orthodontic treatment was highly prevalent, affecting 99.3% of respondents (n = 135) ([Table 3](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t003)). The PI was the most prevalent domain, affecting 83% of respondents (n = 113), followed by the DSC domain (n = 112; 82.4%), the SI domain (n = 83; 61%), and the AC domain (n = 74; 54.4%). In terms of severity, the mean total PIDAQ score was 52.5, whereas the mean scores for each domain were 16.8 for the DSC, 16.7 for the SI, 14.2 for the PI, and 4.8 for the AC domains.

In terms of the extent of impacts, 14% (n = 19) reported significant effects on all domains, 19.9% (n = 27) on three domains, 16.9% (n = 23) on two domains, 27.2% (n = 37) on one domain, and 22.1% (n = 30) reported no significant effects on any domains ([Table 4](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t004)). On average, respondents were affected by 1.8 domains.

**Table 4.**

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

About 22.1% of respondents had low self-esteem. The mean self-esteem score among all respondents was 24.7 (S.D. = 6.3), with a median score of 25.0 (IQR = 8.75) ([Table 5](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t005)). Respondents between the ages of 40 and 49 years old have the highest mean level of self-esteem (28.5) compared to those who are between 30 and 39 years old and from 20 to 29 years old, who have mean scores of 25.2 and 25.4, respectively ([Table 4](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t004)). Even if the mean of both age groups was almost the same, the self-esteem of respondents between the ages of 20 and 29 years old has a median of 26.0, which is slightly higher than the median of respondents between the ages of 30 and 39 years old (24.0). The age group from 10 to 19 years old had the lowest self-esteem in comparison to all the age groups, with a mean score of 23.1. However, the one-way ANOVA of the person measure values found no significant differences in the self-esteem between patients of the different age groups (F (132, 3) = 1.793; p = 0.152). The self-esteem scores between male (mean = 24.0, median = 25.0) and female respondents (mean = 25.1, median = 24.5) were almost similar ([Table 5](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t005)). The independent t-test showed no differences in the self-esteem scores between genders (p > 0.05).

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

[Figure 1](#fig_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-f001) shows that individuals with moderate need (grade of 3) for treatment have a greater self-esteem level than respondents with little need (grade of 2) and severe need (grades of 4 and 5). Self-esteem did not significantly differ between PIDAQ domains and self-rated IOTN-AC assessments of SPM. The Kruskal–Wallis test found that the self-esteem of patients seeking orthodontic treatment were different in regard to the different levels of severity of malocclusion, as measured using IOTN-DHC (p < 0.05). A post hoc analysis by Mann–Whitney tests showed significant differences in self-esteem scores between those with little need and moderate need (p = 0.032) and between moderate need and severe need (p = 0.029) for orthodontic treatment.

**Figure 1.**
Comparison between self-esteem and malocclusion-severity levels, as measured by the Dental Health Component of the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN-DHC).

According to Pearson correlation coefficient ([Table 6](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t006)), self-esteem had a moderately negative correlation with SI (r= −0.425, p < 0.01), a weakly negative correlation with PI (r = −0.321, p < 0.01), a weakly negative correlation with reversed DSC (r = −0.298, p < 0.01) domains, a weakly negative correlation with education level (r = 0.217, p < 0.01), and a weakly negative correlation with age (r = 0.185, p < 0.05). On the other hand, neither gender, professionally rated IOTN-DHC, nor self-reported IOTN-AC was significantly correlated with self-esteem.

**Table 6.**
Pearson correlations between domains of PIDAQ with age, gender, and education level.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

According to the regression analysis ([Table 7](#table_body_display_healthcare-12-01576-t007)), the nine predictors explained 23% of the variance (R2 = 0.28, F (9, 126) = 5.483, p < 0.001). The SI (β = −0.386, p < 0.001), AC (β = 0.228, p < 0.05), and reversed DSC (β = −0.195, p < 0.05) domains were found to significantly predict self-esteem. In this model, other factors, such as PI, self-rated IOTN-AC, professional-rated IOTN-DHC, age, gender, and education level, did not significantly predict self-esteem.

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1. Prevalence, Extent, and Severity of PIDAQ among Patients Seeking Orthodontic Treatment

This study found that PIDAQ prevalence and severity were higher than in previous epidemiological studies on young adults [[28](#B28-healthcare-12-01576)] and schoolchildren [[6](#B6-healthcare-12-01576)]. Our respondents’ mean PIDAQ score was similar to that in a longitudinal study assessing the PIDAQ of patients prior to fixed appliances therapy [[7](#B7-healthcare-12-01576)]. Another study assessing PIDAQ after one year of orthodontic treatment also showed similar pre-treatment scores as this current study, with a significant reduction in the mean values after one year in treatment [[29](#B29-healthcare-12-01576)]. This proves that patients who seek orthodontic treatment have a strong psychosocial impact of their malocclusion and, hence, a worse quality of life compared to individuals who perceive themselves as having no or minimal malocclusion.

The respondents of this study experienced similar impacts on both DSC and PI domains. Other studies found PI to be the most prevalent, but in terms of the extent of impact, we had similar results [[6](#B6-healthcare-12-01576),[28](#B28-healthcare-12-01576)]. This suggests that adolescents and adults seeking orthodontic treatment are more psychologically impacted by malocclusion.

### 4.2. Self-Esteem and PIDAQ

Our study found an association between self-esteem and the PIDAQ domains, with SI having a moderate negative association with self-esteem (r = −0.425; p < 0.05), followed by PI (r = −0.321; p < 0.05). On the other hand, DSC and AC had a weak association with self-esteem, as found by a weak negative association between the reverse-scored DSC with self-esteem (r = −0.298; p < 0.05) and between AC with self-esteem (r = −0.159; p < 0.05). Our findings were similar to studies on the Croatian and Chinese populations [[19](#B19-healthcare-12-01576),[30](#B30-healthcare-12-01576)]. A study among university students also reported that individuals experiencing substantial psychosocial effects due to dental aesthetics are likely to exhibit lower levels of self-esteem [[31](#B31-healthcare-12-01576)]. This suggested that, regardless of cultural differences in the Western or Eastern community, negative social behaviors and dissatisfaction over one’s own dental aesthetics might influence the subjective impressions of an individual, such as self-esteem.

SI, AC, and reverse scored DSC domains were significant predictors of self-esteem in our study based on the regression model analysis. People with higher self-esteem have lower results in the SI domain, which explains that they care less about their dental appearance in social settings. However, people with higher self-esteem have higher results in the AC domain, which means that they are more aware of their physical appearance. Additionally, people with higher self-esteem have lower results in the reversed DSC domain, depicting that satisfaction with dental appearance has a positive effect on self-esteem [[19](#B19-healthcare-12-01576)]. Although the PI domain and self-esteem are correlated, the domain did not significantly predict self-esteem in our study.

### 4.3. Self-Esteem and the Degree of Malocclusion

Our study found no correlation between malocclusion severity and self-esteem, with respondents with little need of treatment having the lowest self-esteem and those with moderate treatment need having the highest self-esteem levels. Research suggests that self-esteem is a complex issue that is not solely dependent on malocclusion [[32](#B32-healthcare-12-01576),[33](#B33-healthcare-12-01576),[34](#B34-healthcare-12-01576),[35](#B35-healthcare-12-01576)], and contentment with one’s appearance can boost self-esteem [[36](#B36-healthcare-12-01576)].

Poor dental aesthetics can increase patients’ levels of anxiety, particularly those with high tendencies toward perfectionism. The constant concern over the teeth can increase their levels of depression [[37](#B37-healthcare-12-01576)]. Luo et al. (2021) suggested incorporating psychological intervention as part of patient management to properly improve the patients’ aesthetic orientation, reduce their expectations, and increase their satisfaction.

Being female and having poor dental aesthetics are factors for poor self-esteem [[38](#B38-healthcare-12-01576)]. On the other hand, orthodontic treatment is an important factor that can improve the self-esteem of adolescents [[38](#B38-healthcare-12-01576)]. A study found that orthodontic treatment improves self-esteem as early as 3 months into treatment and continues to increase after a year’s follow-up [[39](#B39-healthcare-12-01576)]. Other studies also similarly found patients having higher self-esteem levels post-treatment compared to pre-treatment and during treatment [[40](#B40-healthcare-12-01576),[41](#B41-healthcare-12-01576)].

In another study, it was found that global self-esteem remains stable throughout orthodontic treatment. This study found an interaction effect between time into treatment with age and gender for certain self-esteem subscales. For the scholastic competence subscale, the values reduce in girls, while in boys, the values increase during treatment until the end of treatment. Adolescents who started orthodontic treatment at a younger age have been found to have increased levels in the physical-appearance and global self-worth subscales after one year of treatment, whereas older adolescents showed a trend toward decreased self-esteem; however, at the end of treatment, both groups had similar levels of self-esteem [[42](#B42-healthcare-12-01576)].

These findings suggest that self-esteem is influenced by various elements, such as body image, facial appearance, levels of anxiety and depression, and social acceptance.

### 4.4. Self-Esteem of Various Age Groups, Gender, and Education Levels

According to the findings of our research, there is a correlation between increasing age and increased level of total self-esteem, supporting the finding of a previous longitudinal study [[43](#B43-healthcare-12-01576)]. People generally become more accepting of who they are as they get older [[44](#B44-healthcare-12-01576)]. Nonetheless, it should be kept in mind that the trajectory of self-esteem change may differ across cultures [[45](#B45-healthcare-12-01576)] and the environment that one is exposed to.

The current study found no significant difference in self-esteem between genders, despite previous research showing lower self-esteem in adolescent girls [[46](#B46-healthcare-12-01576),[47](#B47-healthcare-12-01576),[48](#B48-healthcare-12-01576),[49](#B49-healthcare-12-01576)] and that malocclusion had a greater impact on girls’ self-esteem [[47](#B47-healthcare-12-01576)]. However, male self-esteem rises, and female self-esteem falls from early adolescence to early adulthood [[50](#B50-healthcare-12-01576)]. Another local study found that males and females in urban areas had similar PIDAQ scores, while males in sub-urban and rural areas had lower PIDAQ scores than their female counterparts [[28](#B28-healthcare-12-01576)]. This finding explained why our current study has no significant differences between the genders, as our respondents were from urban areas of Kuala Lumpur and Selangor.

Our research indicates that an individual’s self-esteem increases with his or her education level, consistent with a previous study indicating higher self-esteem among those with higher education [[51](#B51-healthcare-12-01576)].

### 4.5. Study Limitations

The study faced limitations due to short data collection time and five missing data samples. Despite this, the final sample size was sufficient for power. A majority of the respondents were adults between 20 and 29 years old (52.2%), followed by the combination of adolescents and young adults of between 10 and 19 years old (33.8%). Despite the wide age range of the respondents, their self-esteem scores were generally stable, with no significant differences across the age groups. Therefore, the results of this study could be applied to a wide age group.

## 5. Conclusions

The prevalence of psychosocial impacts of dental aesthetic amongst patients seeking orthodontic treatment was 99.3%, with 22.1% showing low self-esteem. The significant predictors of self-esteem of orthodontic treatment-seeking patients were found to be Social well-being, Aesthetic Concern, and Dental Self-Confidence.

args.key_excerpts: The psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics of patients seeking orthodontic treatment was highly prevalent, affecting 99.3% of respondents, Study found that Domains of the psychosocial impact of dental aesthetics act as predictors of self-esteem in orthodontic treatment-seeking patients, Social Impact, Aesthetic Concern, and Dental Self-Confidence are the factors that significantly contributed to explaining the variation in self-esteem, accounting for, 3.9%, 2.3%, and 2.0%, respectively, The entire model explained 23% of the variation in self-esteem
args.summary: This is a scientific article titled "Dental Aesthetics and Self-Esteem of Patients Seeking Orthodontic Treatment," published in *Healthcare* (2024, Vol. 12, Issue 16, 1576) by researchers from Universiti Malaya, Malaysia. The study investigated the relationship between patients' perceptions of their dental aesthetics and self-esteem among 141 new orthodontic patients (136 respondents, 96.5% response rate). Using the Malaysian Psychosocial Impact of Dental Aesthetics Questionnaire (PIDAQ), Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES-M), and the Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN), the cross-sectional survey found that 99.3% of respondents experienced psychosocial impacts from dental aesthetics, with 22.1% exhibiting low self-esteem. Multiple linear regression revealed that three PIDAQ domains—Social Impact, Aesthetic Concern, and Dental Self-Confidence—significantly predicted self-esteem, explaining 23% of the variance. Social Impact accounted for 3.9%, Aesthetic Concern for 2.3%, and Dental Self-Confidence for 2.0% of the variation. Neither clinician-rated malocclusion severity nor self-perceived malocclusion severity significantly predicted self-esteem. The study concluded that psychosocial impact domains of dental aesthetics serve as predictors of self-esteem in orthodontic treatment-seeking patients, with implications for incorporating psychological assessment in orthodontic treatment planning.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Abstract

### Background

Orthodontic treatment has become significantly more accessible in recent decades, contributing positively to patients’ quality of life by enhancing dental aesthetics and self-esteem. This study aims to investigate how social media usage affects self-esteem, self-perceived aesthetics, and the perceived need for orthodontic treatment among these generational groups.

### Materials and methods

This cross-sectional observational study included 250 participants from three generational groups: Generation Z (born 1997–2012), Generation Y (born 1980–1996), and Generation X (born 1965–1979). Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire distributed through social media platforms. The questionnaire covered background characteristics, patterns of social media usage, self-perceived aesthetics, orthodontic treatment need, and self-esteem. A Visual Analog Scale (VAS) was used for self-perceived attractiveness and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) to evaluate self-esteem.

### Results

The sample comprised 250 participants. Generation Z reported the highest average daily social media use (4.42 h), followed by Generation Y (3.28 h) and Generation X (2.65 h). Social media had a significantly greater impact on the work or studies of Generation Z compared to the other generations. Regarding social comparison, generation Z had a significantly higher tendency to compare their body appearance and life experiences than Generations Y and X. Regarding self-perceived dental aesthetics and orthodontic treatment need, although not statistically significant, Generation X reported the highest perceived need for orthodontic treatment, followed by Generation Y and Generation Z. Self-esteem scores did not differ significantly among generations. Generation Z recorded the lowest mean self-esteem score.

### Conclusion

There were no significant generational differences in perceived orthodontic treatment needs. However, Generation Z exhibited higher social media usage and greater social comparison regarding body image and life experiences, indicating that social media may contribute more significantly role in shaping social pressures among younger generations. In addition, individuals with lower satisfaction in dental aesthetics perceived a higher need for orthodontic treatment.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Introduction

In recent decades, orthodontic treatment has become accessible to a larger portion of the population [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR1)]. This expansion is due to several factors, including improved access to oral health care, driven by preventive approaches in modern dentistry, greater population longevity, better access to information, increased aesthetic expectations in society, advancements in orthodontic technology, and reduced treatment costs in certain countries [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR2), [3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR3)].

The positive impact of orthodontic treatment on patients’ quality of life has been well-documented. After completing orthodontic therapy, children, adolescents, and adults show improved body image and enhanced confidence in their appearance, which contributes to reduced anxiety in social situations and has a favorable effect on their self-esteem [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR4), [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR5)]. Although, self-esteem and aesthetics self-perception is a complex feature and involves several factors such as internalized opinions from others, adherence to cultural norms, social comparisons, social interactions, educational background, and personality traits [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR6)]. Physical characteristics that influence self-esteem include factors such as height, weight, physical attractiveness, and malocclusion [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR7)]. Dental aesthetics significantly contribute to overall physical attractiveness, adolescents with malocclusion have been found to have lower self-esteem scores and experience more significant negative psychosocial impacts compared to those without malocclusion [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR8), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR9)].

Self-esteem, defined as a sense of adequacy stemming from positive self-evaluations and favorable comparisons to others, has been consistently linked to higher levels of body and aesthetic satisfaction [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR10)]. Self-esteem has been identified as being influenced by parental and peer factors, with mass media and social media emerging as the most significant predictors of body dissatisfaction [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR11)]. Self-esteem negatively correlates with social media use, indicating that more frequent use is associated with lower self-esteem [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR12)]. Individuals with lower self-esteem are more likely to engage in social media which can lead adverse effects such as self-isolation, neglect of personal relationships, an increased risk of psychological issues like depression and loneliness, as well as sleep and dietary disturbances, resulting in dissatisfaction with both personal and social relationships [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR13)].

It is clear that internet plays a significant role in modern life, transforming many traditional forms of communication and affecting the orthodontics world [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR14), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR15)]. However, its impact on different generations remains unclear. The generations X, Y and Z were born in different contexts, Generation X (1965 and 1979) grew up witnessing the rise of technology in their everyday lives and significant changes in global events, Generation Y (1980 and 1996) were exposed to the digital world early in their lives, Generation Z (1997 and 2012) the first generation to grow up entirely in an Internet-driven world, shaping their perception of information access and worldview in ways unlike those of previous generations [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR16), [17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR17)].

Malocclusion and dental misalignment can negatively affect mastication, speech, and temporomandibular joint function, potentially leading to discomfort and impaired oral health-related quality of life [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR18)]. Beyond the psychosocial benefits associated with an improved smile, orthodontic treatment plays a critical role in enhancing oral function, maintaining periodontal health, and preventing long-term dental complications [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR19)]. These functional aspects must be considered when evaluating the overall impact of orthodontic care on patient well-being.

Hence, the present study aims is to investigate how social media affects self-esteem, self-perceived aesthetics, and the perceived need for orthodontic treatment across different generations. The null hypothesis states that there is no significant difference in the impact of social media usage on self-esteem, self-perceived dental appearance, or orthodontic treatment need among Generation Z, Generation Y, and Generation X.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Materials and methods

This is a cross-sectional observational study. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the university (CAAE 77741824.5.0000.0020). All participants provided their digital consent prior to the use of their data. The study was conducted in full accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

### Sample calculation

A sample size calculation was conducted to determine the number of participants required for the study. Based on the Brazilian population, treated as an infinite population, a target sample size of 268 individuals was established. This calculation considered a 95% confidence level and a 6% margin of error, with Z = 1.96 representing the value on the standardized normal distribution for a 95% confidence interval, e denoting the margin of error set at 0.05, and p representing the standard deviation of 0.5.

For this study, the population was divided by convenience in three groups, Generation X, refers to those born between 1965 and 1980; Generation Y, also known as the Millennials, born between 1980 and 1996, and Generation Z are individuals born between 1997 and 2012 [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR20)]. Each generation possesses its own distinct identity, but can also be defined by unique collective traits shaped by the world in which they were born and have experienced throughout their lives.

### Questionnaire

A self-administered questionnaire was created in the Qualtrics digital platform (Salt Lake City, UT, USA) aiming to evaluating 1 - Background characteristics and Social Media usage; 2 - Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need; 3– Self-esteem.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Background characteristics and social media usage

For the background characteristics, it was asked 1– Birth date; 2– Sex; 3– Estimated time spend daily in social media; 4 - Have you used social media so much that it negatively impacted your work/studies?; 5 - I compared my body or appearance with that of others; 6 - I compared my life or experiences with those of others.

Questions 4, 5 and 6 were based on previous studies [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR21), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR22)] and evaluated through a 5 point Likert scale (0 - Strongly Disagree, 1 - Disagree, 2 - Neither Agree nor Disagree, 3 - Agree, 4 - Strongly Agree).

### Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need

Regarding Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need the following questions were asked, 1 - Do you currently feel the need for orthodontic treatment? (0: No need for treatment − 100: Extremely high need for treatment); 2 - How satisfied are you with the appearance of your teeth? (0: Not satisfied − 100: Extremely satisfied). The validity and reliability of VAS 100 points VAS scores was described in [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR23)].

### Self-esteem

The fourth part, the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) was employed to evaluate self-esteem levels. This 10-item Likert scale involves respondents rating items on a 4-point scale, ranging from “strongly agree” (SA) to “strongly disagree” (SD). Out of the 10 questions, half are positively phrased, while the other half are negatively phrased. Scoring is as follows: SA = 3, A = 2, D = 1, and SD = 0. Notably, items 2, 5, 6, 8, and 9 are reverse scored (SA = 0, A = 1, D = 2, SD = 3). The summation of scores across the 10 items provides the average self-esteem for each respondent. Scores falling below 15 indicate low self-esteem, those between 15 and 25 suggest moderate self-esteem, and scores ranging from 26 to 30 signify high self-esteem. The scale is validated in English [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR24), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR25)] and was applied in Portuguese [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR26)].

The questionnaire was originally administered in Portuguese. Both the original Portuguese version and its English-translated equivalent are available as supplementary material.

### Data collection

Data collection was conducted by distributing the questionnaire link through social media platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp, using the Qualtrics digital platform (Salt Lake City, UT, USA) during March and April of 2024 in the Brazilian territory. The questionnaire was sponsored with the only geographical restriction being its distribution within X (omitted for review purposes) territory. The questionnaire was accessible from June 02, 2024, to June 10, 2024, and participants could complete it digitally using a computer, smartphone, or tablet. The survey was provided solely in Portuguese, allowing all Portuguese speakers who received the link to participate.

Participants were selected for the study based on specific inclusion criteria: age above 15 years and under 59, consent to participate, and completion of all questionnaire items. Those who did not meet these criteria were excluded. A total of 297 responses were recorded, and after applying the inclusion criteria, 47 individuals were excluded, resulting in a final sample of 250 participants.

### Data analysis

The raw data were extracted from Qualtrics software and organized using Microsoft Excel, where it was compiled and quantified into an electronic database (Microsoft, Inc., Redmond, WA, USA). The quantified data were then exported to SPSS software version 25 (IBM, Armonk, USA) for statistical analysis. Descriptive statistics were used to calculate the mean and standard deviation for numerical variables, as well as the total count and percentage for qualitative variables. For comparing dependent variables among groups, one-way ANOVA and chi-square tests were employed. A significance level of 5% (_p_< 0.05) was used. The data collection and analysis process adhered to the terms and conditions governing the data source.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Discussion

The null hypothesis was rejected for social media impact and accepted for self-perceived dental appearance, orthodontic treatment need, and self-esteem, once the study concludes that social media does have a differential impact across generations, with Generation Z being the most affected in terms of social media usage. This may be attributed to their higher social media usage, increased exposure to curated online content, and a greater tendency toward social comparison [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR17)]. These findings highlight the significance of considering the impact of social media when addressing issues related to body image and self-comparison, particularly among younger populations.

Generation X, Generation Y and Generation Z each have distinct characteristics shaped by their experiences with technology and societal shifts. Generation X, often known as the “forgotten generation,” grew up witnessing the emergence of technology and global changes, may be considered as moderately ethnically diverse [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR27)]. Generation Y, on the other hand, were among the first to grow up immersed in the digital world, earning the label of “Digital Natives” alongside. This exposure has made them adept at using smartphones, tablets, and social media, they engage in multitasking with technology while learning actively rather than passively. Generation Z, meanwhile, is the first generation to grow up entirely in an internet-driven environment, which profoundly affects how they access information and shape their worldview. Generation Z prefers rapid and graphically rich information, reflecting an active and participatory learning style similar to Generation Y [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR28), [29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR29)]. Their deep immersion in technology is often linked to reduced attention spans, marking a unique challenge for this generation compared to their predecessors [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR29)].

Those differences may be seen in the results of this study, once the Generation Z consistently reported spending more time on social media and experiencing a greater impact on their work or studies due to social media compared to Generations Y and X. Additionally, Generation Z exhibited higher levels of social comparison related to body image and life experiences, suggesting that social media may exert more social pressure on younger generations. However, no significant differences were found between generations regarding satisfaction with dental appearance, perceived need for orthodontic treatment, or overall self-esteem scores. This indicates that these aspects are more influenced by individual perception rather than generational differences.

The findings of this study highlight generational differences in social media usage, social comparison, and perceptions related to orthodontic treatment and self-esteem. Generation Z reported significantly higher daily use of social media compared to Generations Y and X, which aligns with prior literature suggesting that younger generations are more heavily engaged with digital platforms [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR20), [30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR30)]. The increased use of social media in Generation Z also correlated with a significantly greater impact on their academic and work performance. The heightened scores for comparing body appearance and life experiences observed in Generation Z imply that this generation may be more susceptible to the negative influences of social media [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR9)]. This aligns with the Pearson correlation analysis, which found a weak negative correlation between self-esteem and social comparison tendencies, reinforcing the idea that excessive comparison may contribute to lower self-esteem values [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR31)]. In addition, this has been linked in prior studies to poorer well-being outcomes, such as increased depressive symptoms and anxiety Increases in Depressive Symptoms, Suicide-Related Outcomes, and Suicide Rates Among U.S. Adolescents After 2010 and Links to Increased New Media Screen Time [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR32), [33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR33)] These differences are particularly concerning as they emphasize how social media contributes not only to social pressures but also to self-perceived inadequacies among younger populations.

Regarding orthodontic treatment needs and self-perceived aesthetics, there were no significant generational differences, which suggests that the perceived need for orthodontic intervention and satisfaction with dental appearance are likely influenced more by individual factors rather than generational characteristics. However, Generation X reported the highest perceived need for orthodontic treatment, while Generation Y showed the highest satisfaction with dental appearance. This may be linked to differences in access to orthodontic care or aesthetic expectations among these groups. In terms of self-esteem, the analysis showed no significant difference between generations, although Generation Z had the lowest mean self-esteem score. Interestingly, the Pearson correlation analysis revealed that individuals with higher tendencies to compare their bodies and life experiences with others had lower overall satisfaction, suggesting that social comparison is an important factor affecting personal well-being [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR34), [35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR35)].

Additionally, the analysis of gender differences revealed that female participants compared their body appearance and life experiences with others significantly more than male participants, which aligns with existing research that suggests social media exerts a more pronounced effect on females [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR36)]. The results of this study support these findings, as higher social comparison scores among female participants correlated with greater dissatisfaction with self-perception, suggesting that social media may act as a reinforcing mechanism for aesthetic insecurity. This phenomenon is particularly concerning given the documented links between excessive social comparison, depression, and self-worth issues [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR37)]. In contrast, male participants reported lower social comparison scores, consistent with prior studies indicating that men, on average, experience less external pressure regarding physical appearance from social media [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763#CR38)]. Despite no significant differences found between genders in terms of orthodontic treatment need, satisfaction with their smile, or time spent on social media, the findings underscore the importance of understanding gender-specific influences on social comparison and self-perception. Females seem to be more vulnerable to the pressures of social media and its impact on body image, potentially leading to greater well-being challenges.

A cross-sectional study applied only to the Brazilian population has certain limitations that affect its broader applicability. The findings may lack generalizability to other cultural contexts, limiting the ability to draw conclusions beyond Brazilian). Additionally, this type of study captures data at a single point in time, making it difficult to establish causal relationships or understand changes over time. These factors highlight the need for cautious interpretation and, ideally, validation through longitudinal or more diverse studies. In addition, the recruitment through social media may have introduced selection bias, favored frequent users, limiting representation of less active individuals. Also, this study is subject to recall bias, as participants may have estimated rather than accurately reported their time spent on social media. Additionally, the uneven sample distribution, with a higher proportion from Generation Z and the notable gender imbalance in the sample may have influenced self-esteem outcomes, may have impacted the statistical power of comparisons. Furthermore, this study did not account for moderating factors such as socioeconomic status, education level, or personality traits, which may influence self-esteem and social media engagement. Moreover, this study did not aim to diagnose self-esteem issues or any other psychological condition and applied a simple approach to the self-esteem questionnaire and time spent on social media. Future research should integrate these variables for a more comprehensive understanding of digital engagement and self-perception.

Although, future research could investigate how social support, digital literacy, and resilience strategies might help reduce the negative effects of social media on self-esteem and aesthetic perception separate by generations. The results in this study indicate a need for interventions that focus on reducing social comparison and promoting healthier engagement with social media, particularly among young females, to improve digital well-being.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12220763)Conclusion

There were no significant generational in perceived orthodontic treatment needs, indicating a similar recognition of orthodontic intervention requirements across Generations X, Y, and Z. Individuals who were less satisfied with their dental aesthetics consistently perceived a higher need for orthodontic care, emphasizing the role of self-perception in determining orthodontic needs. Social media usage and its perceived impact varied significantly across generations, with Generation Z reporting the highest daily use and a significantly greater impact on their academic and professional performance. Additionally, Generation Z exhibited a stronger tendency toward social comparison, both in terms of body image and life experiences, compared to Generations Y and X.

The social media may exert a more substantial influence on social pressures among younger generations. Frequent social comparisons of body image are closely linked to broader life comparisons. Lower satisfaction with dental aesthetics was directly associated with a greater perceived need for orthodontic intervention, emphasizing the importance of self-perception in orthodontic decision-making processes.

args.summary:
This article presents a cross-sectional study published in BMC Oral Health (2025) investigating how social media usage affects self-esteem, self-perceived dental aesthetics, and perceived need for orthodontic treatment across three generations. The study included 250 Brazilian participants: Generation Z (born 1997–2012, n=141), Generation Y (born 1980–1996, n=69), and Generation X (born 1965–1979, n=40). Data was collected via a self-administered questionnaire distributed through social media platforms, using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for self-perceived attractiveness and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) for self-esteem.

Key findings: Generation Z reported the highest average daily social media use (4.42 hours), significantly more than Generation Y (3.28 hours) and Generation X (2.65 hours). Generation Z also reported significantly greater negative impact of social media on work/studies and higher tendencies to compare their body appearance and life experiences with others compared to the other generations. No statistically significant differences were found among generations regarding self-perceived dental aesthetics, perceived orthodontic treatment need, or self-esteem scores. However, Generation Z recorded the lowest mean self-esteem score (21.84). A strong positive correlation (r=0.733) was found between comparing one's body and comparing life experiences. A moderate negative correlation (r=-0.489) existed between satisfaction with dental appearance and perceived need for orthodontic treatment. Female participants compared body appearance and life experiences significantly more than males. The study concludes that while there were no significant generational differences in perceived orthodontic treatment needs, social media appears to exert more social pressure on younger generations, particularly Generation Z.

# The impact self-esteem towards the orthodontic issues in the social media: a cross-sectional study

* Open Access
* 01.12.2025
* Research

Erschienen in:
[![Link zu Zeitschrift BMC Oral Health](https://assets.springermedizin.de/resource/img/journal_cover_placeholder.svg)](/bmc-oral-health-1-2025/50413588)

## Abstract

### Background

Orthodontic treatment has become significantly more accessible in recent decades, contributing positively to patients’ quality of life by enhancing dental aesthetics and self-esteem. This study aims to investigate how social media usage affects self-esteem, self-perceived aesthetics, and the perceived need for orthodontic treatment among these generational groups.

### Materials and methods

This cross-sectional observational study included 250 participants from three generational groups: Generation Z (born 1997–2012), Generation Y (born 1980–1996), and Generation X (born 1965–1979). Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire distributed through social media platforms. The questionnaire covered background characteristics, patterns of social media usage, self-perceived aesthetics, orthodontic treatment need, and self-esteem. A Visual Analog Scale (VAS) was used for self-perceived attractiveness and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) to evaluate self-esteem.

### Results

The sample comprised 250 participants. Generation Z reported the highest average daily social media use (4.42 h), followed by Generation Y (3.28 h) and Generation X (2.65 h). Social media had a significantly greater impact on the work or studies of Generation Z compared to the other generations. Regarding social comparison, generation Z had a significantly higher tendency to compare their body appearance and life experiences than Generations Y and X. Regarding self-perceived dental aesthetics and orthodontic treatment need, although not statistically significant, Generation X reported the highest perceived need for orthodontic treatment, followed by Generation Y and Generation Z. Self-esteem scores did not differ significantly among generations. Generation Z recorded the lowest mean self-esteem score.

### Conclusion

There were no significant generational differences in perceived orthodontic treatment needs. However, Generation Z exhibited higher social media usage and greater social comparison regarding body image and life experiences, indicating that social media may contribute more significantly role in shaping social pressures among younger generations. In addition, individuals with lower satisfaction in dental aesthetics perceived a higher need for orthodontic treatment.

## Introduction

In recent decades, orthodontic treatment has become accessible to a larger portion of the population [[1](#CR1)]. This expansion is due to several factors, including improved access to oral health care, driven by preventive approaches in modern dentistry, greater population longevity, better access to information, increased aesthetic expectations in society, advancements in orthodontic technology, and reduced treatment costs in certain countries [[2](#CR2), [3](#CR3)].

The positive impact of orthodontic treatment on patients’ quality of life has been well-documented. After completing orthodontic therapy, children, adolescents, and adults show improved body image and enhanced confidence in their appearance, which contributes to reduced anxiety in social situations and has a favorable effect on their self-esteem [[4](#CR4), [5](#CR5)]. Although, self-esteem and aesthetics self-perception is a complex feature and involves several factors such as internalized opinions from others, adherence to cultural norms, social comparisons, social interactions, educational background, and personality traits [[6](#CR6)]. Physical characteristics that influence self-esteem include factors such as height, weight, physical attractiveness, and malocclusion [[7](#CR7)]. Dental aesthetics significantly contribute to overall physical attractiveness, adolescents with malocclusion have been found to have lower self-esteem scores and experience more significant negative psychosocial impacts compared to those without malocclusion [[8](#CR8), [9](#CR9)].

Self-esteem, defined as a sense of adequacy stemming from positive self-evaluations and favorable comparisons to others, has been consistently linked to higher levels of body and aesthetic satisfaction [[10](#CR10)]. Self-esteem has been identified as being influenced by parental and peer factors, with mass media and social media emerging as the most significant predictors of body dissatisfaction [[11](#CR11)]. Self-esteem negatively correlates with social media use, indicating that more frequent use is associated with lower self-esteem [[12](#CR12)]. Individuals with lower self-esteem are more likely to engage in social media which can lead adverse effects such as self-isolation, neglect of personal relationships, an increased risk of psychological issues like depression and loneliness, as well as sleep and dietary disturbances, resulting in dissatisfaction with both personal and social relationships [[13](#CR13)].

It is clear that internet plays a significant role in modern life, transforming many traditional forms of communication and affecting the orthodontics world [[14](#CR14), [15](#CR15)]. However, its impact on different generations remains unclear. The generations X, Y and Z were born in different contexts, Generation X (1965 and 1979) grew up witnessing the rise of technology in their everyday lives and significant changes in global events, Generation Y (1980 and 1996) were exposed to the digital world early in their lives, Generation Z (1997 and 2012) the first generation to grow up entirely in an Internet-driven world, shaping their perception of information access and worldview in ways unlike those of previous generations [[16](#CR16), [17](#CR17)].

Malocclusion and dental misalignment can negatively affect mastication, speech, and temporomandibular joint function, potentially leading to discomfort and impaired oral health-related quality of life [[18](#CR18)]. Beyond the psychosocial benefits associated with an improved smile, orthodontic treatment plays a critical role in enhancing oral function, maintaining periodontal health, and preventing long-term dental complications [[19](#CR19)]. These functional aspects must be considered when evaluating the overall impact of orthodontic care on patient well-being.

Hence, the present study aims is to investigate how social media affects self-esteem, self-perceived aesthetics, and the perceived need for orthodontic treatment across different generations. The null hypothesis states that there is no significant difference in the impact of social media usage on self-esteem, self-perceived dental appearance, or orthodontic treatment need among Generation Z, Generation Y, and Generation X.

## Materials and methods

This is a cross-sectional observational study. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of the university (CAAE 77741824.5.0000.0020). All participants provided their digital consent prior to the use of their data. The study was conducted in full accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

### Sample calculation

A sample size calculation was conducted to determine the number of participants required for the study. Based on the Brazilian population, treated as an infinite population, a target sample size of 268 individuals was established. This calculation considered a 95% confidence level and a 6% margin of error, with Z = 1.96 representing the value on the standardized normal distribution for a 95% confidence interval, e denoting the margin of error set at 0.05, and p representing the standard deviation of 0.5.

For this study, the population was divided by convenience in three groups, Generation X, refers to those born between 1965 and 1980; Generation Y, also known as the Millennials, born between 1980 and 1996, and Generation Z are individuals born between 1997 and 2012 [[20](#CR20)]. Each generation possesses its own distinct identity, but can also be defined by unique collective traits shaped by the world in which they were born and have experienced throughout their lives.

### Questionnaire

A self-administered questionnaire was created in the Qualtrics digital platform (Salt Lake City, UT, USA) aiming to evaluating 1 - Background characteristics and Social Media usage; 2 - Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need; 3– Self-esteem.

## Background characteristics and social media usage

For the background characteristics, it was asked 1– Birth date; 2– Sex; 3– Estimated time spend daily in social media; 4 - Have you used social media so much that it negatively impacted your work/studies?; 5 - I compared my body or appearance with that of others; 6 - I compared my life or experiences with those of others.

Questions 4, 5 and 6 were based on previous studies [[21](#CR21), [22](#CR22)] and evaluated through a 5 point Likert scale (0 - Strongly Disagree, 1 - Disagree, 2 - Neither Agree nor Disagree, 3 - Agree, 4 - Strongly Agree).

### Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need

Regarding Self-perceived attractiveness and orthodontic need the following questions were asked, 1 - Do you currently feel the need for orthodontic treatment? (0: No need for treatment − 100: Extremely high need for treatment); 2 - How satisfied are you with the appearance of your teeth? (0: Not satisfied − 100: Extremely satisfied). The validity and reliability of VAS 100 points VAS scores was described in [[23](#CR23)].

### Self-esteem

The fourth part, the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) was employed to evaluate self-esteem levels. This 10-item Likert scale involves respondents rating items on a 4-point scale, ranging from “strongly agree” (SA) to “strongly disagree” (SD). Out of the 10 questions, half are positively phrased, while the other half are negatively phrased. Scoring is as follows: SA = 3, A = 2, D = 1, and SD = 0. Notably, items 2, 5, 6, 8, and 9 are reverse scored (SA = 0, A = 1, D = 2, SD = 3). The summation of scores across the 10 items provides the average self-esteem for each respondent. Scores falling below 15 indicate low self-esteem, those between 15 and 25 suggest moderate self-esteem, and scores ranging from 26 to 30 signify high self-esteem. The scale is validated in English [[24](#CR24), [25](#CR25)] and was applied in Portuguese [[26](#CR26)].

Anzeige

The questionnaire was originally administered in Portuguese. Both the original Portuguese version and its English-translated equivalent are available as supplementary material.

### Data collection

Data collection was conducted by distributing the questionnaire link through social media platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp, using the Qualtrics digital platform (Salt Lake City, UT, USA) during March and April of 2024 in the Brazilian territory. The questionnaire was sponsored with the only geographical restriction being its distribution within X (omitted for review purposes) territory. The questionnaire was accessible from June 02, 2024, to June 10, 2024, and participants could complete it digitally using a computer, smartphone, or tablet. The survey was provided solely in Portuguese, allowing all Portuguese speakers who received the link to participate.

Participants were selected for the study based on specific inclusion criteria: age above 15 years and under 59, consent to participate, and completion of all questionnaire items. Those who did not meet these criteria were excluded. A total of 297 responses were recorded, and after applying the inclusion criteria, 47 individuals were excluded, resulting in a final sample of 250 participants.

### Data analysis

The raw data were extracted from Qualtrics software and organized using Microsoft Excel, where it was compiled and quantified into an electronic database (Microsoft, Inc., Redmond, WA, USA). The quantified data were then exported to SPSS software version 25 (IBM, Armonk, USA) for statistical analysis. Descriptive statistics were used to calculate the mean and standard deviation for numerical variables, as well as the total count and percentage for qualitative variables. For comparing dependent variables among groups, one-way ANOVA and chi-square tests were employed. A significance level of 5% (p < 0.05) was used. The data collection and analysis process adhered to the terms and conditions governing the data source.

## Results

The study sample consists of a total of 250 participants, with 75 males (29.6%) and 175 females (70.4%). The mean age of Generation Z was 21.57 years, 141 participants, including 43 males (29.8%) and 98 females (69.5%), Of these, 112 participants (79.4%) had received or were actively undergoing orthodontic treatment, while 29 participants (20.6%) had never undergone such treatment. Generation Y reported a mean age of 31.12 years, 19 males (27.5%) and 50 females (72.5%). Among these participants, 57 individuals (82.6%) have undergone or are currently undergoing orthodontic treatment, whereas 12 participants (17.4%) have not. Generation X has a mean age of 46.13 years, 40 participants, including 13 males (32.5%) and 27 females (67.5%). Of these participants, 31 individuals (77.5%) have undergone or are currently undergoing orthodontic treatment, and 9 participants (22.5%) have not.

When analyzing the average time spent daily on social media across three different generations, Generation Z spent significant more hours the (4.42 h) then Generation Y, whose mean was (3.28 h) (p = 0,005), and Generation (2.65 h) (p < 0,001). (Table [1](#Tab1)). In the analysis of the social media questions, the results show that Generation Z reported a statistical significantly higher impact of social media on their work or studies (mean = 2.74) compared to Generation Y (mean = 2.33) and Generation X (mean = 2.08), (p-value of 0.002). Regarding the comparison of body or appearance with others, Generation Z had a significant higher score (mean = 2.33) compared to Generation Y (mean = 1.78) and Generation X (mean = 1.58), (p < 0.001). Similarly, for comparing life or experiences with others, Generation Z had a higher mean (mean = 2.31) compared to Generation Y (mean = 1.81) and Generation X (mean = 1.68), with significant differences observed between the groups (p < 0.001). (Table [2](#Tab2))
